subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext:
First I should like to say to the Prime Minister that we are glad to see him back in the house. We were disturbed yesterday when the flag at 24 Sussex street was flying upside down. But in all sincerity I would like to say how very glad we are to see him back.
Now I wish to ask the right hon. gentleman a question arising out of press dispatches this morning to the effect that at the dominion-provincial conference the premier of Quebec insisted on Canada pension plan premiums to the extent of 4 per cent instead of the proposed 2 per cent as the price of its agreement to an amendment to the British North America Act permitting survivors and disabled to be included in the plan. The information has not been available to the house, and I now ask the Prime Minister to tell the house what actually took place and whether or not this statement represents the situation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by thanking my right hon. friend for his welcome back to the house and to assure him that the flag was upside down at Sussex street only because of sympathy for myself, inasmuch as I felt a little upside down yesterday.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext: So it was intentional?

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext:
In so far as the question is concerned, the report in the Globe and Mail to which my right hon. friend refers, and which indicates that widows, orphans and invalids are at present included in the Canada pension plan, is inaccurate and based on a misstatement of the published facts about the Canada pension plan. The report, as I have just indicated, says that pensions for disabled people and for younger widows and orphans are at present included in the Canada pension plan.
That, Mr. Speaker, is not the case. The plan as described to the house on July 18 and subsequently, the plan as it has been discussed with the provinces, does not provide pensions for people below the age of 65. It does not require a constitutional amendment. It may be that in the future, if there is a plan in effect, steps can be taken along these lines and those steps would require a constitutional amendment. But that is not the case with the present plan, and there has been no discussion with the provinces of an alteration in the plan to that effect. No constitutional amendment is required for the plan that has been put to the house and to the provinces, and no province has ever claimed any veto over this plan as it has been put forward.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I then ask the Prime Minister to advise the house now whether Premier Lesage insisted on Canada pension plan premiums totalling 4 per cent instead of 2 per cent.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext: No, Mr. Lesage did not insist on any such thing.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare on July 18, although she made it clear these other items were not included in the Canada pension plan, referred to them as matters to be discussed
5872	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry with the provinces, may I ask whether Mr. Lesage related the two in any way at the recent conference?

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS AT CONFERENCE RESPECTING AMOUNT OF DEDUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated a moment ago the government hopes that in due course the plan can be extended in the way that has been suggested in this article to cover widows with dependent children, orphans and disabled contributors, and the possibility of a future extension of the plan in that direction has been discussed with the provinces. This would require a constitutional amendment, and certain provinces have agreed to such a constitutional amendment in the future after the plan is in effect. But all the provinces have not agreed. The province of Quebec has not agreed to that yet, and the matter is still under discussion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Favreau (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope you will convey my apologies to the Speaker for having stood up for more than 30 seconds, as I did a few minutes ago, instead of just bowing when he was desperately trying to introduce the government motion pertaining to Indian affairs. It was a slight case of inexperience and absentmindedness.

Mr. Chairman, it has not been the practice of the house, when considering the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, to have a general discussion when the departmental administration vote is called. In the past it has been agreed, both by those who have held this portfolio and by members of the committee, that the most effective way of handling the estimates is to provide for discussion of each main area of the department's activities as the first item in that particular area is reached. These areas are the estimates of the citizenship and immigration branches on the one hand and Indian affairs on the other.
To follow this course, I believe, will facilitate the committee's consideration of a department whose activities are diverse and complex, ranging from the Yukon Territory to Cape Breton within our borders, and from Dublin to Hong Kong beyond our shores.
While the range of responsibilities of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is a broad one, there is a common unity of purpose which binds it together. Each branch of the department is concerned with the most valuable and by far the most complex of our resources: our human resources.
The immigration branch selects future citizens for our country. The two citizenship branches encourage and assist newcomers to reach the status of Canadian citizenship, and the Indian affairs branch is dedicated to assist the Indians to achieve full citizenship.
As the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, expressed it in 1949 when the department was formed:
Having citizenship and immigration and Indian affairs in one department would indicate that the purpose of the activities of that department was to make Canadian citizens of those who were born here, of the original inhabitants of the territory, or those who migrated to this country.
I should like at this time to acknowledge the great contribution made by the officers and staff of the department in all its branches.
Despite the great distances which separate many of the activities at home and abroad and despite the variety of responsibilities, the 28902-5-374
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration members of the department seem to share in the common purposes and objectives which provide the basis of their organization. I have found that they are competent, that they work hard and that they are dedicated to the best traditions of the public service.
To make progress in the best way, let us start by discussing the first item on citizenship vote 5, the citizenship registration branch. I shall make a statement on citizenship and immigration, covering the general field of votes 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35, after which other members may make their general comments.
When the citizenship and immigration items are completed, we will then repeat the process when the first item is reached on the Indian affairs votes, leaving departmental administration to the end.
With the concurrence of the committee then, Mr. Chairman, I suggest we leave vote 1 and turn to votes 5 to 35 inclusive.
Do I have the consent of the committee?

The Canadian Citizenship Act came into force on January 1, 1947, and provides for the legal status of Canadian


citizens. The act is administered almost entirely by the Canadian citizenship registration branch, which has an establishment of 96 at headquarters in Ottawa, and 64 in the citizenship courts situated in various centres in Canada. The most recent citizenship court was established in Ottawa in March of 1963. There are nine other courts in Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton, London, Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Moncton and Windsor.
These, along with the regularly constituted courts, provide facilities for persons wishing to apply for Canadian citizenship. In addition, 56 persons have been appointed to act as courts for the purpose of the Canadian Citizenship Act in remote areas. Four similar appointments have been made overseas for the assistance of servicemen.
At this point I would like to inform the hon. members who have expressed an interest in the qualifications which must be met by an applicant for Canadian citizenship, that a review is at present being made of the standards required of applicants from the inception of the Canadian Citizenship Act to the present time, with a view to establishing as far as it is possible uniform criteria across Canada.
In 1962, 72,080 persons became Canadian citizens. This is the third highest number for any one year, the highest being in 1957 when 95,462 certificates were granted, and the second highest is 1958 when 84,183 grants were made. From January 1, 1947 to December 31, 1962 a total of 654,379 persons have been granted citizenship in Canada. In addition, 389,586 certificates were issued to persons who wished to have proof of their status as Canadians.
It has been ascertained that approximately 40 per cent of the immigrants who entered Canada in the 10 year period 1953 to 1962 who are eligible for Canadian citizenship have become Canadians. Fitting and appropriate ceremonies for the presentation of certificates of citizenship can provide a most important symbol of the benefits to new Canadians and to others also of the acquisition of Canadian citizenship. For this reason consideration is being given to expanding the number of courts. Plans are at present being considered for the establishment of a court of Canadian citizenship in Calgary. Through these media and through appropriate publicity it is hoped to encourage a greater number of people to apply for Canadian citizenship.
With respect to the Canadian citizenship branch, it is responsible for two main programs; first, developing a greater degree of understanding of Canadian citizenship and of group relations amongst newcomers, Indians and Canadians generally through advisory and financial assistance to organizations and

agencies engaged in citizenship education and community action; and second, for immigrant instruction by providing textbooks to provincial departments of education and others conducting classes for adult newcomers, and by providing matching grants to provincial and territorial governments for citizenship and language teaching costs.
The increase in this vote is minimal, about 3.5 per cent. It results almost entirely from the larger amount provided for payments to provinces for the conduct of language classes for immigrants. For such classes the federal government matches the contributions made to local school boards by the provincial governments. The increase results from higher teachers' salaries and increased efforts to reach immigrants in remote areas, housewives and hospitalized newcomers, and to develop language courses within the vocational retraining programs for immigrant workers. The only other allotment which has increased over the past year is salaries, up about 2 per cent as a result of the salary revisions. There have been no increases in staff.
There is one development in particular which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. As hon. members are aware, persons of Indian status and ancestry have been moving to urban areas in rapidly increasing numbers during recent years. In general, Canadian communities have been quick to respond to the needs of these people, and their adjustment has been aided considerably by the establishment of friendship centres in a number of urban communities. The first of these centres was organized in Winnipeg in 1957 and eight more have been added since that time. Last year new centres were started in Toronto, The Pas, the Battlefords, Prince Albert and Edmonton. Interest in friendship centres is increasing. It is hoped and expected that many others will be organized within the next few years.

I should like at this time to outline some thoughts of the government on immigration matters and a few developments which have taken place since I took office several months ago.
That Canada should continue to encourage immigration is self-evident; people from other lands make a positive contribution to our nation's economic and social well-being. There are considerations of national interest for encouraging immigration and there are other more human considerations, such as family re-union, the reduction of discrimination based on origin or creed and the acceptance of charitable and humanitarian re-28902-5-374J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration sponsibilities. Through immigration we can do much to abolish antagonisms and to foster understanding.
Our manpower needs are changing and the needs of other countries are changing with conditions and circumstances. For this reason, immigration policies should be reviewed fairly frequently. There is another reason as well: it has been established for many years that immigration to Canada is not a fundamental human right, but a privilege, and that mass immigration should take into consideration the general economic and social factors of Canada.
With these considerations in mind, the government in 1963 has continued the policy initiated by the previous government early this year of pursuing a more aggressive program. It has been difficult to increase the flow of immigrants, but a beginning has been made.
During the first 10 months of this year, 79,628 immigrants arrived in Canada, and I expect that by the end of 1963, there will be about 92,000. This compares favourably with the 1961 and 1962 totals of 71,689 and 74,586 respectively. Our objective for next year is to revert to the pre-1959 figures of well in excess of 100,000, the exact number to be determined by the response to improved methods of recruiting immigrants of suitable types.
During the past months, we have been conducting an intensive study of immigration policy and procedures. We have particularly concerned ourselves with Canada's economic requirements for manpower and population and with Canada's humanitarian responsibilities. As for immigration from an economic viewpoint, we have concluded that it should consist mainly of young, skilled workers and of entrepreneurs with the capital and experience needed to become established in their own self-operated enterprises in Canada. Such persons fit into our economy and society with little or no difficulty and, far from taking employment away from Canadians, they can be instrumental in helping create jobs for unskilled Canadian workers.
To obtain such immigrants, the department will pursue a vigorous informational and promotional program in the countries which have traditionally been our principal sources, such as the United Kingdom, France and the U.S.A. To this end we intend to open two offices in France, in addition to that which has been at Paris for many years, if the necessary arrangements can be made with the French authorities.
We shall continue to provide service to immigrants in other parts of the world as interest and volume warrant. In this respect,
5880	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration we have recently established permanent offices in Cairo and Madrid, and an officer has been assigned to Beirut on a temporary, experimental basis.
In countries where our offices are not located, travelling teams of trained immigration officers will continue to make periodic visits to assess the qualifications of individual applicants and determine their suitability as future Canadian residents. So far this year, officers who visited the West Indies and central and South American countries, have selected 1,139 persons on the basis of individual merit. Travelling officers have also selected 1,106 persons living in various Pacific islands and countries in the Middle East.
With respect to humanitarian immigration, we have continued to give recognition to Canada's position as one of the more prosperous countries in the world community, by providing for special movements of persons in a refugee or quasi-refugee situation, as a result of war or other disaster.
To illustrate, 217 refugees sponsored by reliable persons were admitted during the first 10 months of this year, even though the immigrants could not meet the normal occupational requirements for admission, and arrangements are being completed for an additional 192 refugees in similar circumstances.
Also, Canada as a special project, in cooperation with the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, undertook to settle 24 physically or socially handicapped refugees. They have now been settled in employment by immigration staffs and I am happy to say are doing well. In addition to such special movements, of which these are but two, approximately 1,000 refugees have come individually for settlement; and I am at the moment giving consideration to a pilot project for the movement of 100 families from Hong Kong in co-operation with the council of churches.
It is important to achieve the best possible integration of policies relating to employment and to immigration, in the light of the most reliable economic studies that can be made.
Arrangements are in progress to establish an interdepartmental committee of senior officials of interested departments to assess the economic aspects of immigration policy on a continuing basis and to advise my department in this respect.
In the course of reviewing our policies I have also been attempting to bring the Immigration Act and regulations more into line with changes which have taken place in our economic and social environment and with advances in the field of medicine. This is a many-sided, complex and sensitive area. I am reviewing very carefully representations which have been made to me concerning

certain of the immigration regulations which on their practical effect can create arbitrary distinctions in the privileges of sponsorships which are enjoyed by Canadian citizens.
Moreover, I shall be introducing within the next few days a system for assessing settlement arrangements for sponsored immigrants according to standard criteria. This should do much to clarify the requirements and obligations of sponsors and thus eliminate most of the uncertainty which has existed with respect to the matter in the past.
Finally, plans for integrating customs-immigration primary inspection at border ports of entry have been put into effect, with total savings to date of almost $300,000. In carrying out our integration plans, we have taken care to ensure that no immigration or customs officer at present employed will be deprived of his job.
This terminates my introductory statement concerning the citizenship and immigration branches.
May I turn now to the various problems affecting Indian affairs.

In introducing discussion of the estimates of the Indian affairs branch I should like to pay tribute to my immediate predecessors in office, who maintained and developed many of the basic programs initiated prior to 1957 and who, in turn, laid the foundation for many worth-while projects which we shall be moving forward as quickly as possible.
I wish also to thank members from all sides of the house who have written and spoken to me about ideas and suggestions and who have sent forward constructive criticisms. Many of the members have shown their interest by well taken and searching questions, either put orally or placed on the order paper. This non-partisan interest and concern for the welfare and advancement of Indians has been heartwarming and encouraging for me in taking up the responsibilities of superintendent general of Indian affairs. I am confident we can continue to work together effectively in our efforts to find the best means of assisting the Indians of Canada to make the difficult adjustment required to meet the demands of a bewildering and complex time.
Indeed, it is only if we all work together in this house, and with the full co-operation and support of the provinces, municipalities, churches, voluntary agencies and private efforts of Canadian citizens, that success can be expected for the Indians. There are no single measures on which we can rely for a solution of the problems involved. The task calls for hard work and sacrifice. We must be ready to accommodate ourselves to the

legitimate demands of the Indians, and to recognize and respect the different values and aspirations inherent in their culture. We must go much further and create bonds of confidence and mutual respect. We must listen as well as speak, and learn before we attempt to teach.
We know from experience here and abroad that doing things for people, giving them gifts and granting them favours, brings many evils; complacency and patronage on the part of the giver, dependency and loss of confidence for the receiver. Our primary task, then, must be to provide opportunities for the Indians to help themselves. At present many Indians rely heavily upon the federal government and upon the protective and restrictive provisions of the Indian Act for their economic and cultural survival.

I thank the committee. We must make it possible for them of their own free will and in their own time, to regain selfconfidence, to maintain pride of race and achieve control under their own leadership. This result, when attained, will eliminate the need for special programs, special legislation and special services. As long as these are required, the goal of independence on an equal footing with other Canadians will not have been accomplished.
Not the least of the needs we face is a new look at Indian legislation. We are proceeding to review the Indian Act as quickly as a sound and thorough consideration will permit. Our objective in amending the act will be to give the Indian people a stronger voice in the conduct of their own affairs. The emphasis will be on Indian initiative and responsibility, and a loosening of the paternalistic ties. We also propose to follow the practice first begun in 1951, and repeated in 1955, of consulting Indian groups and bands before this new legislation is passed.
Another matter requiring attention is the establishment of an Indian claims commission. The joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Indian affairs recommended that such a commission should be established to hear matters of long standing concern and grievance to Indians. A resolution to introduce this legislation is now on the order paper, and it is my hope that this resolution will pass and that the bill will be given first reading before the house rises.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Once this is done I intend to send the proposed legislation providing for the disposition of Indian claims to the Indian bands and organizations across the country for study and consideration.
One of the most encouraging aspects of Indian affairs today is the interest being taken by the provinces and provincial agencies in the welfare of the Indian people. I refer to the provincial and local school board co-operation that is enabling thousands of Indian children to attend integrated schools; to the increasing participation of Indian bands in provincial social and economic assistance programs; to the co-operation received from provincial governments in the road building program for Indian reserves; and to other examples of provincial interest and action which I shall mention further on in the course of my remarks. Also I acknowledge the very welcome aid being given by various private agencies who join with us in a desire to better the future for fellow Canadians of the Indian race.
Last month, for the first time in Canadian history, the question of Indian affairs was discussed at a federal-provincial conference. I am glad to report a large measure of agreement. It was agreed that Indians should be associated more closely with the life of other Canadians and that Indians have full equality of opportunities. It was recognized that the time has come to find the basis on which the widest possible range of federal, provincial and municipal services currently provided to non-Indians can be extended to Indians, and that the Indians must be consulted throughout. It was agreed that a further meeting should be held, if possible by May 1964, at which provincial ministers and their senior officials would discuss with us this whole question in greater detail. Preparation and planning for this next meeting is now under way. I sincerely believe that through this new development we are entering a new phase and have reached a turning point in the field of Indian affairs in Canada.
A sound body of knowledge is essential to the continuing development of effective programs. The government, therefore, is sponsoring a Canada-wide Indian research program. In announcing this undertaking in the house on December 2 last I mentioned that the study, conducted by social scientists from the universities, would cover four major areas concerning Indians; economic development; advancement in education; responsibilities that exist at various government levels; and band councils and the development of selfgovernment. In addition to the main areas of research, a number of supplementary studies would be made on related subjects.

Basic to our efforts is the willingness of the Indian people to carry themselves forward. The great majority, I am certain, are determined to take advantage of every opportunity provided to them for advancement.
Opportunity requires sound training, both academic and technical. The 1963-64 estimates for the Indian affairs branch reflect the emphasis on education in that 57.1 per cent of the amount requested is designated for education purposes, including an amount of $25,294,810 for the administration, operation and maintenance of the school program and $5,792,000 for capital expenditures. There is an increase this year in the operation vote attributable to an over-all increase in enrolment and an expected rise in education costs for Indian children attending non-Indian schools. The number of children enrolled in non-Indian schools now exceeds 18,500, or almost 40 per cent of the Indian school population.
A scholarship program for Indian students has been continued from previous years with encouraging results. In addition other financial assistance, including the payment of tuition fees, was given to 3,344 students to enable them to complete high school, university and vocational training courses. Indian parents, too, are showing greater interest in education. There are now 40 Indian school committees which are in effect embryonic school boards, and which constitute a basic step toward Indian responsibility for the operation of schools on reserves.
Efforts toward the inclusion of Indians in welfare programs of the provinces must be continued and intensified. It is recognized that there is also a need for the establishment of services designed to help those residing in Indian communities to provide for their own needs. The establishment of such services is now under active consideration.
The opportunities for mature and competent Indian men and women, prepared to give leadership in the reserve community and elsewhere, are constantly broadening. Emphasis is being placed on training programs to enable Indians to develop more fully their potential capacity for leadership roles. Utilization of training facilities and resources offered by various governmental and private organizations has made possible marked expansion in this field.
Economic development programs are vital. In agriculture, provision is being made to continue and expand the practice of lending cattle on rotation to selected Indians. Agricultural conferences to stimulate interest and improve the methods used by Indian farmers have been successfully undertaken, and Indian farmers are being encouraged to avail


themselves of the services offered by the federal and provincial departments of agriculture.
The number of selected Indians placed in permanent employment, with the co-operation of the national employment service, is growing year by year and has now reached a total of 1,617, including 477 in 1962-63. In addition there were over 5,000 rural and seasonal placements made last year with assistance from the national employment service. This does not include the many Indians who obtained employment independently or with assistance from their local agency superintendent.
Extensive assistance is provided those Indians who still pursue their traditional vocations of hunting, trapping and fishing, and harvesting wild crops. A ten year agreement with the province of Ontario concerning renewable resources development has completed its first year of operation and shows promise. Similar programs are being carried on in other provinces by formal agreement, as in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, or under informal working arrangements. Notable in the latter case are joint surveys of the renewable resources potential in British Columbia and Quebec.
The value of handicraft production as a supplementary source of income is recognized by inclusion in the estimates of an amount to provide for instruction and supervision, the furnishing of raw materials, and the purchase and sale of finished handicraft items.
Another matter of importance is the expanding economy of the Indians is the development of forest resources on Indian reserves. Provision is made in the estimates for forestry investigations and for the continuing costs of reforestation.
Various measures by which the government seeks to alleviate distress caused by seasonal declines in employment are being applied on Indian reserves throughout the country. Indian bands are participating in the municipal winter works incentive program and, up to the the end of November, 43 applications from Indian bands, totalling $143,000, had been approved. In addition 70 projects amounting to $383,000 will be carried out on Indian reserves located within designated development areas. A further 650 projects, totalling $1,200,000, have been provided for under a special Indian community employment program for bands which lack the funds to enable their participation in the winter works incentive program.
In all economic programs an effort is being made to involve Indians in planning and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
management, by recruiting as much as possible from the ranks of the bands concerned the help required to carry on day to day supervision, and by submitting proposals to band councils before programs are undertaken. It is hoped that through experience gained by these means, Indians will qualify for permanent positions in the activities of the economic development division and gradually take over management of their own affairs.
The need for more and better roads to facilitate access from Indian reserves to neighbouring non-Indian communities is recognized in the estimates. Such access is becoming increasingly important as the integrated school program proceeds. Similarly the adjustment of Indians to the general economy requires free movement between the reserves and centres of employment and marketing. Also recognized is the need for adequate water and sewage facilities in Indian communities. Substantial amounts will be expended for improving these services. Concurrently, emphasis will be placed on education campaigns designed to enlist the co-operation of Indian bands in improving sanitation facilities on the reserves.
In conclusion may I emphasize that the programs which I have outlined have one main purpose in mind; to assure the greatest possible measure of opportunity, equality and well-being for the Indian people. To be successful we need not only the assistance of all levels of government but also of voluntary organizations, private individuals and the general public, and above all the active support, co-operation and assistance of the Indian people themselves.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's somewhat lengthy statement because I believe, as he does, that this is a very interesting department indeed. I am glad he has enlightened us to some extent with regard to what he intends to do within the next year. I noted with interest that the minister was not at all pleased with the number of immigrants who had been admitted to Canada in the last three or four years and that the Liberal party is now embarking upon a program whereby some 100,000 or more immigrants will be asked to come to Canada in 1964. The minister did say specifically that advertising and immigration programs would be undertaken in countries such as the United Kingdom, France and the United States. He also said that the requirements for admission to Canada would be the same as those drafted by that very able minister of citizenship and immigration, Mrs. Ellen Fairclough, who unfortunately is no longer in this house.
I am wondering, of course, whether the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration intentionally overlooked the question of immigration from other countries. I say this because during the last election and shortly after numerous press reports in the country indicated that the minister was going to change the Immigration Act to favour the admission to Canada of Chinese in particular. In view of these promises I think we should have heard something today about these proposed changes. I hope that during the course of the afternoon he will be able to enlighten us in this regard.
I feel I would be remiss in my duty, Mr. Chairman, if I did not say that I sincerely believe the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is endeavouring to do a good job in his department. I have handled a number of immigration cases from my constituency and others, by reason of my ethnic background, so I have had considerable dealings with the minister and I thank him for his co-operation. At the same time I want to deal with some aspects of the act that I think are unnecessary or at least, to be less unkind, very dangerous.
I wish to deal specifically with two cases. One is the Weldon Chan case. Newspaper articles of as late as June 3 last indicate that the minister is going to determine what is to be done with this particular family. The following is reported in the Calgary Herald of June 3 last:
Before reaching a final decision, the immigration department wili have to re-examine the Chan case thoroughly.
Every one of us in this house knows there is sufficient evidence on file and sufficient evidence available to enable the minister to determine what is to happen to this particular family in the matter of a day or two. What concerns me is that I remember well what happened in this department when the present Secretary of State, who is not in the chamber at the present time, was in charge. I tell the minister that we will be watching these developments very closely. If there is any suggestion that some of the moves the minister has made-although I agree with him at the moment-have been made for political purposes, as has been the case in the past, I will be the first to question them in this House of Commons.
The second case, which is very similar indeed to the Chan case, is that of Irene Rebrin of Vancouver. I understand this young lady was also promised that something would be done with regard to her status in Canada. She was promised that her case would be reviewed very soon. This promise was made by the minister early in May. This is now December 14, and Irene Rebrin of Vancouver still does
5884	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration not know what is her status in Canada. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister only because we were bitterly criticized for our alleged lack of concern in these cases, and it appeared to a great many people in Canada that if the Liberals were in fact elected they would look after these matters immediately. As I pointed out earlier, some of these promises were made in May of this year; it is now December and we have heard no more about them. I hope the minister in his remarks this afternoon will enlighten us with respect to these two matters.
The other matter that I touched on very briefly a moment ago was the promise of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to change the Immigration Act to favour Chinese immigrants. An article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of September 24 last has this to say:
Sweeping changes to regulations governing the admission to Canada of Chinese immigrants were forecast Monday night by immigration minister Favreau.
He also told a meeting of the Canadian Chinese community that he plans to visit Hong Kong later in the year to investigate problems associated with the movement of Chinese immigrants from that city to Canada.
Mr. Favreau said he intends to "seek a fair and just solution to the vexing problem of Chinese immigration to Canada".
This statement was made in September of 1963. Has the minister now visited Hong Kong; and if he has, unknown to me, what were the results of that visit?
I now wish to deal with the act. It appears that some of the more difficult applications for admission which over the last three or four years were refused by the Conservative government have been approved in recent weeks. They have been approved under section 8(1) of the Immigration Act which, just to enlighten the house, reads as follows:
The minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada or, being in Canada, to remain therein.
Since amendments are contemplated to the Immigration Act, I wonder whether it would not be advisable for the minister to consider a complete review of this particular section and to refer it, indeed to refer the entire act, to a committee so that some degree of unanimity would be reached as to a change which would be acceptable to the house. I think a change is required in this act which would favour the admission into Canada of people from any country in the world.
The other section I want specifically to deal with is section 31(d) of the regulations. I spoke about this in 1959, and it is the section dealing with the admission of people from behind iron curtain countries. This section cites a long list of countries to which


it is applicable, and I am dealing in particular with Ukrainians and Poles, people from that particular part of Europe. Unfortunately under this section there is an age limitation of 21 years. I realize that we must take into account our security, our health, and I suppose many other factors; but I suggest to the minister that since he is using his discretionary powers under section 8, and in view of the many requests for admission to Canada of people over the age of 21 by childless relatives in this country, could the minister not use his powers of discretion in this regard? I say again that I do not like this power of discretion section and would like to see it eliminated; therefore I would also like to see section 31(d) amended.
I want to deal specifically with the problem under subsection (d) of section 31 of the regulations. I have in my city at least four cases of Polish, Ukrainian and Russian people who are childless and who have estates ranging from $25,000 to $150,000. Because these people are childless they made application to adopt a nephew or niece living in Poland or somewhere behind the iron curtain. We will not admit these people to Canada at the present time because they cannot qualify by reason of age. In one particular instance which occurred about three or four weeks ago a hotel owner who had made application for admission to Canada of one of his nieces died shortly after having made the application, which was refused on the ground that there was no provision under the existing regulations for the admisison of such a person. What will happen in this particular case? The hotel and estate are probably worth $150,000 at least. In this instance there are no other living relatives of this deceased man in Canada, so I suppose the money which accrues from the estate will go to Poland, will it not? In the light of what I have said I think certain changes are necessary and should be considered by the minister.
There are many other sections of the act with which I wish to deal, but we are very anxious to get on with the estimates. I understand there is a lengthy list of speakers on Indian affairs, and I do not want to detain the committee any longer than absolutely necessary. However, I do want to bring to the attention of the minister one more matter which comes under the Canadian Citizenship Act. It concerns section 18, which states in effect that a Canadian citizen who is not Canadian born may lose his Canadian citizenship if he has resided out of Canada for more than a period of ten years.
The position into which that section puts an immigrant Canadian is this. Let us suppose that a young chap emigrated to Canada

and obtained a job with an international corporation. Although this man would be a Canadian citizen in due course of time he could not take a permanent posting in a foreign country and still remain a Canadian citizen were he to remain in that country longer than ten years. I suggest most sincerely that section 18 of the citizenship act should be repealed.
May 1 conclude by saying that I hope the minister will be in a position to answer some of the questions I have posed to him this morning. I know there will be other questions coming from the floor, and he will be in a position to deal with them more fully as time goes on.

Mr. Chairman, the subject of immigration is one of very great human interest as well as economic interest. It affects the rights of a great many Canadians who have come to this country, and many more who will come from all parts of the world; people who come here to aid in the development of the Canadian economy and to enrich the culture of Canada.
In opening my remarks I should like to compliment the minister and to congratulate him on his appointment and on the way he is carrying on his duties. I have had a good deal to do over the years with the department of immigration, sometimes in what might be called an adverse, if not a hostile, fashion; but I should like to pay tribute to the sympathy and to the liberal-with a small "1"- attitude with which the minister and his staff and officials have dealt with many cases of hardship which are from time to time called to his attention.
I want to congratulate the minister on some of the excellent speeches he has made on the subject of immigration. I have particularly in mind a speech he made on September 13 of this year to the annual meeting of the real estates agents of the province of Quebec. In that speech the minister dealt most effectively with the widespread myth that immigrants put Canadians out of jobs. I think we should nail that fallacy, because it just is not so. In fact, as the minister pointed out at that time, the more than two million immigrants who have come to Canada since the end of the first world war have brought to this country an immense addition of capital and skill.
The minister gave an example in the course of his speech. He pointed out that between 1952 and 1962 more than 9,000 of them established businesses of their own and paid $116 million for those businesses, creating employment for 45,000 people. He also pointed out in his speech that more than $1,117 million had been infused into the Canadian economy between 1946 and 1962 by immigrants in addition to nearly half a million dollars worth of 28902-5-375

I have complimented the minister, but in case he should think I intend to continue in this vein indefinitely let me tell him right now that there are grave deficiencies in our Immigration Act and in the regulations governing the admission of immigrants to this country, as well as in administration. I was glad to hear the minister say that this question was under active review-I think that was the phrase he used-and that changes would be made. I know the hon. gentleman has been in office for only eight months. I know he has been handicapped by the fact that during part of that period he had no deputy minister. I might, in passing, congratulate him on the acquisition of Mr. Isbister as deputy minister. But there are these difficulties.
Let me try to summarize them. In my view racial discrimination remains both in the act and in the regulations. I intend to deal with this matter later on. We have, and I say this advisedly, farcical immigration proceedings. There is a lack of elementary justice about these hearings. We refuse entry on grounds which are not disclosed to the applicant, so that people often do not know why they cannot bring their wives or children into this country. An explanation is refused them. They are told simply that the applicants do not meet the requirements. I know there is an explanation of this, and perhaps the minister will give it to us later, but I still think the position is unsatisfactory. The requirements are so vague that it is often impossible for an immigrant or his sponsor to determine what conditions he has to meet in order to enter this country.
I have summarized some of these deficiencies. Now I want to discuss them in a little more detail. In another of the excellent speeches he made, on this occasion to the Chinese community in Vancouver on September 23 of this year, the minister made a statement with which I am heartily in accord. I am sure it does in fact represent his views on this particular matter. He said:
X have been distressed by the accusations of discrimination which have reached me. If prejudice exists in immigration matters it must be eliminated. True Canadianism permits no discrimination. All citizens are equal in rights and responsibilities regardless of ethnic origin or creed. It is with this view in mind that I am most sincere in my efforts to wipe out discrimination and prejudice.
I accept this as being a sincere expression of the minister's attitude on this matter. However, I wish to point out that so far, in practice, the form of the regulations and the form of Canadian law do not bear out that excellent statement of principle. The

Again that is an admirable statement, but I think it is time we ourselves eliminated certain discriminatory features which are written into our laws. Before we try to cast out the mote in the eyes of our neighbours we should, if I am quoting the scripture correctly, cast out the beam which is in our own eyes. I wish to read one section of the act to see whether it does not fall directly within the condemnation of the Prime Minister with respect to United States legislation. Under section 61 the governor in council is given certain powers. I am not suggesting for one minute that the governor in council would use those powers in an arbitrary way, but the section does give him power to make regulations, among other things-
(g) prohibiting or limiting of admission of persons by reason of
(i)	nationality, citizenship, ethnic group, occupation class or geographical area of origin,
(ii)	peculiar customs, habits, modes of life or methods of holding property.. .probable inability to become readily assimilated
-and so on.
It is we in this parliament who have given power to the governor in council to restrict admission to this country by any order in council or regulation on account of the applicant's ethnic group, the geographical area from which he comes, and so on.
The minister may very well say, "We do not exercise that power; there is no discrimination left in the regulations themselves". I wish that were the case, but it is not the case. One of the former ministers of citizenship and immigration to whom reference has already been made in this debate, Hon. Mrs. Fairclough, used to say, when

certain changes were made in the regulations, that discrimination had been eliminated from the regulations. Unfortunately that is not so.
I think I should explain briefly that there are two main streams of immigration into this country. First there are those admitted under regulation 31 by reason of their education, training and skill. I acknowledge that under this section no sort of discrimination is written into the regulations. But there is another stream of immigration into this country; that is, immigration on what might be called family grounds, the right to bring people in so as to reunite families.
What do we find there? With regard to the right to bring one's relatives into this country we find a clearcut discrimination against people of Asian or African origin. The regulation provides that people who came from any country of Europe, including Turkey, or from any country of North, Central or South America or the islands adjacent thereto, or from Egypt, Israel or Lebanon can bring in a son, daughter, brother or sister, as well as the husband or wife, and the unmarried son or daughter under 21 years of age of such son, daughter, brother or sister. But this list of countries eliminates a not inconsiderable portion of the globe. It eliminates the whole of Asia with the exception of Turkey, Israel and Lebanon. It omits, as I read it, the whole of Africa with the exception of Egypt.
What is the standard with regard to these people? If they wish to bring in their relatives they are far more limited in their power to do so. That discrimination, whatever the reason, remains in the regulations as they exist and are administered at the present time. I suggest that if the excellent words that have been used by the minister himself and the Prime Minister as to the elimination of discrimination are to be carried out in practice as well as in theory, those who come from Japan, China or other parts of Asia or from Africa, from whatever country it may be, should be put in precisely the same position, with regard to their right to bring in members of their family and connections, as those who come from South America, Europe or any other part of the world. I say that until that is done there will remain in the regulations, which are part of the law of this country and for which the government is responsible, the very discrimination which the government says, and I believe sincerely, that it desires to eliminate.
In the limited time I have I am not going to attempt to go into a whole series of cases. My colleague the hon. member for Danforth called my attention to a case that he dealt with where a Chinese gentleman of some substance in the city of Toronto, Mr. Sing

Chong, sought to bring in an orphan granddaughter, 17 years of age, who had got out of China and was in Hong Kong. Her father was dead and her mother had disappeared. He sought to bring the child into the country and he was refused. Why? Because the regulations say that people from that part of the world, no matter what their need is, no matter how appropriate it may be, cannot bring in their grandchildren; but if they came from some other part of the world they would be able to be admitted. My first suggestion then, Mr. Chairman, is that in the amendment of the regulations we should remove the last traces of discrimination that exist therein.
I also spoke of another matter which those who deal with the subject of immigration seldom appreciate. I refer to the question of whether a would-be immigrant or a sponsored immigrant is or is not entitled to have a proper hearing as to the reasons for the refusal of admission into this country. We have spoken a lot about the bill of rights, the right of a person to know what is the case made against him, the right to a fair hearing. We have talked of these things, but we do not practise them in this particular field. Let me say that any unfairness applied to people who seek to come into Canada creates a bitterness that does damage to Canada and to Canada's reputation throughout the world, and in the world of today we cannot afford not to live up to the principles which we expound so eloquently from time to time.
What is the situation in regard to this matter? I have to give a hurried summary, but the basis of the Immigration Act is that under section 5 there is a whole series of prohibitions of people who for one reason or another should not be admitted to this country. No one will complain about the fact that parliament has included these prohibitions, but it is not these prohibitions that are used as the instrument of selection with regard to who shall come into this country. It is that particular prohibition which says that those who fail to comply with regulations passed under the act shall not be admitted, and the control of entry into this country is based upon the existence of certain regulations made by order in council. Only incidentally and occasionally does the department call into effect the prohibitions that are made under the act.
In passing the Immigration Act parliament indicated that a person who sought admission to Canada was entitled to a hearing before an administrative officer with regard to whether he fell or failed to fall within these prohibited classes. But what is the actual practice in respect of this matter? I say that by 28902-5-375i
administrative machinery many of these hearings have been turned into a complete farce because of the regulation that is applied. Even though the government and the department may have some reason for which they wish to exclude a particular immigrant, they do not advance that reason. They do not say anything about it. They say "You do not comply with the regulations because you have not got a visa", or "You have not got a medical certificate" or "You have not got a letter of pre-examination". Where do they get these things? They get them from the department and the department, without giving any reason, refuses to give them these documents they are supposed to have. So these people sit down in a hearing before a special inquiry officer, a hearing directed by parliament under the act, to decide whether or not they have a piece of paper which the department has given them no opportunity to get, which does not mean anything at all, which they know they have refused and intend to continue to refuse. The result is that people about whose health there is no question at all can be and are refused admission in the daily administration of the act on the ground that they do not have a medical certificate. When they ask where they can get a medical certificate they are told "You can get it from a medical officer we appoint, but we will not give you an appointment to find out if there is anything wrong".
I had a case come to my attention just the other day of a Scotswoman who was divorced from her first husband and remarried. Her first husband came to Canada and has lived here a good many years. In the event her second husband also left her but her first husband returned to Scotland on a visit. They resumed what had previously been lawful matrimony but now presumably was a common law union or living in sin. The former wife returned to Canada and has been living with her first husband, but she is now in the process of being deported. Why? Not for any crime she is supposed to have committed, not for any immorality that is alleged against her. I never have thought it particularly immoral for a woman to go back to live with her first husband if her second husband has deserted her. No such reason has been advanced, but rather that she has not got a letter of pre-examination. Nobody ever told her she was supposed to have such a letter. She came to this country as a visitor originally and stayed with her husband. She has a job working in a retail store and her husband has a job. They are perfectly able to look after themselves.
What has happened in this case? First of all she was told she could not come into this country because she did not have a medical

Mr. Chairman, before lunch I was endeavouring to point out what I believed to be some of the weaknesses in the Immigration Act, regulations and practices. I did point out that the regulations were being used in a manner that deprives an applicant of the type of fair hearing that I think parliament contemplated when it passed the Immigration Act, and provision for which was made in a number of sections. The applicant is not given the real reason for the refusal. I do not think it was contemplated that the hearing would be farcical, but rather that it would provide the real reason why the applicant would not be allowed to come into Canada or join with his relatives in Canada.
I should like to add a further point on the right of appeal from the decision of the special inquiry officers. I would suggest that this right of appeal is too restrictive at the present time. I suggest that the appeal tribunal should include at least one person of judicial, as distinct from administrative, position, and further, that it should be given power to make recommendations on compassionate grounds, rather than merely dealing with the legal correctness or otherwise of the inquiry officers' findings. I further suggest that reasons for the decision of the appeal tribunal should be published, so that those concerned with these matters would know the basis upon which the act is being administered.
Another criticism made of the regulations, Mr. Chairman, is their vagueness as to the


standards of admission. For example, regulation 31, which as I said is a key regulation, uses phrases like these: "By reason of education, training, skills or other qualifications, is likely to be able to establish himself in Canada"; "has sufficient means of support to maintain himself in Canada until he has so established himself". The sponsorship requirements contain equally vague language. I was very glad to hear the minister say that in the next few days the established criteria would be published. In my opinion, this is urgently needed because without these criteria the sponsors, the families of those who are brought in, do not know what sort of standard they are supposed to establish. They have hopes, but they have no means of determining how they fail to come up to those required standards, or what they must do to bring themselves within the standards that would enable them to bring their relatives into the country.
I should like to say something about the general economic implications of immigration. We have to recognize that, however desirable increased immigration into Canada might be on general principles, the continuance of large scale unemployment is bound to act as a brake upon immigration. When over 300,000 Canadians or 4.5 per cent of our working force are unemployed, the resistance to increased immigration is both natural, inevitable and to some extent justified. We have to plan for an expanding economy so that we can, in our own interests and in the interests of the world community, welcome a steady and increasing flow of immigrants into this country.
Some time ago, Mr. Chairman, I came across what I thought was an admirable statement of the principles upon which the responsibilities of governments in the field of immigration were based. This statement is taken from the report of a conference sponsored by the world council of churches in June of 1961, held at Leysin, Switzerland. There were represented 75 churches representing 30 countries. With regard to immigration they laid down the following principles:
(a)	The need to avoid any exclusion of migrants on the basis of race, nationality or religion;
(b)	The responsibility to help ease population pressures in situations where feasible migration can make a contribution;
I suggest the British West Indies is an example where that might be applicable so far as Canada is concerned.
(c)	The humanitarian claims of migrants in situations of special hardship;
(d)	The particular claim of the political refugee upon the help of the world community.
I stop there to say that I welcomed what the minister told us about the admission of

refugees. However, I suggest it may be helpful to put in the regulations themselves some discretion on the part of the minister, or perhaps some indication as to the basis upon which refugees might be sponsored and admitted into the country so that the public could know what could be done to deal with this problem. Then, to continue the quotation:
(e)	The vital importance of preserving the family as a unit, making every effort to avoid separating the wage earners from the rest of their families over an extended period and facilitating reunion when members have migrated:
(f)	The responsibility for friendly reception and assistance in the adjustment of the migrant;
(g)	The need to support the efforts of international organizations in the field of migration to increase their scope and effectiveness.
I understand that some years ago Canada withdrew from the United Nations organization that dealt with the problems of migration throughout the world. I suggest the government should take another look at this matter:
(h)	The need for the speedy development of unused economic resources so that each country can make a maximum contribution to the welfare not only of its own citizens, but of those of other lands.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to acknowledge that the minister has told us of an intensive study of immigration procedures, and I would express the sincere hope that we see the results of this study brought into effect before too long. I have read in the newspapers that the minister may possibly be called upon to shoulder other responsibilities. I assure him we wish him well, if that is so; but nevertheless I hope he will stay long enough in his present job to introduce amendments to the Immigration Act and make new regulations which will embody the result of the intensive study which he says is being undertaken.
In conclusion may I summarize the recommendations we would make to the minister:
1.	That the act and the regulations be amended to remove the traces of discrimination that remain, and perhaps I am being polite when I use the word "traces", because I think it is more than that.
2.	That the regulations and practices be changed so as to give would-be immigrants and sponsors the reasons for the refusal of admission.
3.	The abandonment of the practice of using procedural requirements of visas, medical certificates, letters of pre-examination as a means of denying the real hearings contemplated by the act.
4.	The improvement of appeal procedures.
5.	The clarification of the basic standards of admissibility.

No. 6, and this is one I have not mentioned before, is the inculcation in all immigration officials of the expansive and welcoming philosophy which has been so well expressed by the minister himself from time to time, but which sometimes does not seem to permeate to the lower levels of his department.
If these changes are made Canadians will be able to maintain a policy of immigration which remains selective but that is fair in its application, and which will encourage the continued flow of immigrants that will be required if Canada is to attain the prosperity and greatness of which she is capable.

I want to make just a brief reference to the other branches of the department. I think it is rather paradoxical that we have in Canada, I would say, a considerable number of people who come here, take up residence, enter into various activities, earn their living, make their money, but yet never put themselves in the position where they can fulfil their responsibilities of citizenship. We build a glowing picture of the future that is ours.
