In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to suggest that if we are going to achieve the objective of increasing immigration to Canada, and if we are to build up this nation for the future, then we will have to see to it that our monetary and financial policies are adequate to meet the challenge. If we do not make these reforms then we are going to be faced with insurmountable problems in bringing more people into the country. We have to make these adjustments, and I suggest that if we are bold and venturesome enough to move out into this area into which so many are afraid to move, and that if we move forward with resolution and make these necessary monetary and financial changes, then we are going to be able to open our doors and accept an ever increasing number of immigrants from the nations of the world, thereby making a contribution not just to Canada but to the whole world and to humanity in general. It is unreasonable to assume that it is either desirable or proper for us to try and restrain population growth. We should move as quickly as possible in the opposite direction, consistent with the ability of our economy to absorb those who wish to come to this great country. With these observations I yield the floor, because I realize there are many others who want to speak about this seemingly interesting subject about which so much can be said.

Mr. Chairman, a department which employs 5,147 civil servants, its estimates amounting to $67,528,820, is certainly an important department and I congratulate the minister, Mr. Favreau, for having been chosen as its incumbent. In the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the minister and his senior officials must act at all times with great diplomacy and be vigilant regarding the admission into our country of citizens from varied countries of the world.
Mr. Chairman, into the area which I represent, Villeneuve riding, have come a great number of immigrants from Germany, Poland, Ukraine and Sweden. There are also some Danes, Italians, French, Belgians, in short a cross-section of all the nationalities in the world.
The minister and his high officials must study each of the numerous requests they receive from people who want to settle in Canada, in order to prevent, as far as possible, the coming to Canada of subversive and undesirable elements, which happened in some occasions in the past. Therefore, immigration must be selective so that our country will have good people, respectable people, people who will not destroy our customs and our good name, but will increase our country's reputation by taking part in our various economic and social activities.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw the minister's attention to the fact that intensive publicity is made in some European countries to encourage immigrants to settle in Canada. Canada is represented to them as a garden of Eden where they can live without assuming any responsibility but having all advantages that can be possibly imagined.
And as mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), the migrants planning to settle in Canada must be made aware of the responsibilities that they will have to assume after coming to this country. They must also learn to carry out these responsibilities. They must not think that when they are in Canada, they will have nothing else to do but live in pleasant idleness in a garden of Eden where everything will come free.
Mr. Chairman, when immigrants arrive from overseas, they usually are guaranteed a job for a year or two. As a matter of fact, they start working almost as soon as they arrive, while there are thousands of unemployed in this country. All over Canada, we hear our jobless complain about this state of affairs, not because they are against immigrants, but rather against the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which does not take into consideration the economic conditions prevailing in this country, when the government intends to receive 100,000 immigrants per year.
Mr. Chairman, may I refer to my own area as an example. Immigrants arrive with employment contracts in their pockets, which enable them to get a job immediately in one of the mines: Noranda, Bourlamaque, Sigma or Malartic. Try to imagine the reaction of Canadians who have lived in this area for 10, 15 or 20 years and have had to queue up at the unemployment insurance office for a

year or two, because a few mines have closed down. As I said, those Canadian unemployed have nothing against the immigrants, but they have resentment against the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which nevertheless authorizes 100,000 immigrants per year to enter this country when they cannot find jobs in the same industries.
Mr. Chairman, while 100,000 immigrants are coming in annually from different countries of the world, we have this paradoxical situation that, in the meantime, thousands of Canadians cross the border to the south to settle down in the United States. Surely there are reasons which prompt our Canadian fellow citizens to do so, especially at a time when the department is encouraging the immigration of 100,000 persons a year.
Why do Canadians emigrate to the United States? Surely there are basic economical reasons. Our people probably get better salaries in the United States, better employment opportunities, and so they leave Canada, their parish, their province and their friends to settle down in a foreign country. Mr. Chairman, I think the Department of Citizenship and Immigration should take those facts into consideration.
I completely agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) when he says that it would be possible to bring in more immigrants than we are doing, but not at a time when we cannot even guarantee employment and security for our own citizens. If we had an economic system providing for the economic development of Canada, then, I think it would be easy to increase materially the number of immigrants coming to Canada, because I submit everything has yet to be done in our country, we have hardly begun developing its physical possibilities.
If our financial and monetary situation allowed us to begin those developments, security and freedom would be guaranteed to all our citizens within two years, and that, even if we were bringing in more immigrants than we are doing at the present time because then it would be sensible for them to come and live in a new country where everything remains to be done, where natural resources are practically undeveloped.
Mr. Chairman, as far as immigration is concerned, I call the minister's attention on this point: there are Canadians who are not satisfied and unfortunately, some of them blame the immigrants because they think they are taking their jobs. I do not think so. But it is obvious that we will have to try and solve that problem, about which our Canadian citizens are concerned, before going ahead with the immigration program. Our Canadian citizens should be our first concern, they are
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the ones who should get our first consideration. As for the immigrants, let us stop our-immoderate and exaggerated publicity in Europe which leads people to believe that in Canada, they could make a livelihood without facing any responsibility. A few years ago, some Hungarians who had landed in Montreal lost no time in returning to their country because they had been misled over there before deciding to come to Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to dwell on the subject of immigration. I might say, in conclusion, that in our area immigrants behave like gentlemen. I had the opportunity on many occasions to meet in their clubs some Italian, Ukrainian, Polish and German people, and all of them, without exception, felt very much at home in our area. They are good workers who do credit to our district. We need immigrants like those, but I must stress one point: before bringing more immigrants to Canada, let us try at least to look after our own people.
I would like to add a few words about Indians. The Indian affairs branch in Ottawa and the department of natural resources of the province of Quebec seem to disagree on the question whether the Indians living in northern Quebec come under the jurisdiction of Quebec or Ottawa.
My good friend, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) has recently drawn the attention of the house on the small islands situated to the north of the province of Quebec and asked that these islands be granted to the province; the inhabitants of those small islands, whether Indians or Eskimos, would naturally become citizens of the province of Quebec. In northern Ungava, in the James bay area, there are also some Indians. I sincerely think that the minister is looking after their case and is co-operating with them. They need assistance.
A moment ago, an hon. member said that the Indians had been the first owners of our land. He was right. The government's duty is to make it possible for the various Indian tribes to acquire as much knowledge and know-how as possible, while retaining their own traditions and customs; their civilization may not resemble ours, but they have their own culture and education. It is up to us to help them become good citizens, people with confidence in the white man instead of fear. Indians have been taught certain aspects of history, transmitted to them from generation to generation over the years, and they have learned that three or four centuries ago, the white man has not always been very kind to them. Today, let us try to give them faith in us; they are human beings; let us help them to develop within the framework of a state

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration which should be-and this is my closing remark-a shining example of respect for human rights held up for the whole world to see. That example, this parliament in Ottawa, and the Canadian nation, as a whole, are quite capable of giving.

Mr. Chairman, I will be my usual brief self. The minister has had a very easy time of it this morning and this afternoon, and well he should because I think he is one of the most able ministers of the government. I do not very often say things like that.
You do not have much chance.

I am particularly pleased that the minister is going to take a hard and careful look at changes in the immigration regulations. I think he should. The hon. member for Villeneuve has referred to the hesitancy that is prevalent to some extent in this country with regard to allowing immigrants to come to Canada when jobs are being sought by Canadians. However, those of us who have taken part in committees on this matter and who have studied some of the evidence given there, especially in connection with the population explosion in the world, realize the situation that is facing the world.
We should bear in mind that the Malthusian theory of population growth is almost correct for the last 7,000 years and that by 1980 we can expect the population of the United States and Canada to double. As Professor M. Bates has pointed out, every time one's pulse beats the population of the world is increased by one. We have to face the fact that there are a great number of people in the world and that we cannot remain an island unto ourselves. If we do not open the door it will be battered down. What we can do is to make sure that the people who do enter our country are the type we want or are people who can fit into our general scheme of things. No one is going to be able to hold back immigration, because it is just not going to be possible.
I should like to point out that there is some misunderstanding between new Canadians and those who have been here for decades or generations. In many cases I think it is a matter of communication. Communication between citizens is nothing strange to us and we know that if we cannot understand someone there is a feeling of mistrust. I have been in the construction field for several years and I am aware of the fact that the injustices meted out to new Canadians in the period between 1953 and 1956 were in many cases fairly severe. But the immigrant came to Canada without a command of the language and in some cases with very little education. He was a stranger with no money and faced

complete insecurity. When he arrived in this country he was told just about everything and, having no sense of security, no knowledge of the language and not being able to communicate, there was a natural tendency for him to settle in an area where his people or his friends lived, such area being more or less of a ghetto.
We say that once such people are here they must study and learn to speak English but the man with a family has nothing to fall back on and when he is working 14, 15 or 16 hours a day for very little pay in order to make a go of things he has neither the time nor the energy to get a command of the language. And so it goes. Thirty years later he still has no command of the language.
I should like to make this suggestion to the minister. From the time the prospective immigrant, in the country in which he is then living, makes his application for entry to Canada, to the time when a visa is granted, a period of a year to two years generally elapses. Surely it would not cost Canada very much to arrange for instruction of such people in either French or English, depending on where the applicant wants to settle. This could be done right at our legation in the country of a prospective immigrant, or by some other method arranged through the legation. These people are at home. They know they are going to come to Canada after their applications have been processed, and this is the time when they would be most receptive to learning either English or French. I suggest that the cost would be very little. When they came here they would be able to read the newspapers. They would be able to read the regulations and learn that they did not have to work for 50 cents an hour. They would know what the rates were. They would know where they could live and how to get where they wanted to go. I suggest this would bring about closer communication with all other Canadians and I think that half of the problem would be solved. With great respect I submit this suggestion to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that members of the committee have listened with interest to the remarks of the minister in which he outlined the functions and achievements of his department. I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate him on being selected to direct the destinies of this particular department.
My remarks today will relate specifically to the Indian affairs branch and the future of the Indian people of Canada. However, with regard to the citizenship branch I should like to make one brief comment. I am sure we are all extremely gratified to see the ever

increasing number of people who are applying for and receiving Canadian citizenship. In the northern part of our country the situation is no different. Each month we see more and more people from other lands, who have come to our newly developing areas to seek employment, make their homes and bring up their families, applying for Canadian citizenship and being granted this privilege.
The minister dwelt at some length on the achievements of the Indian affairs branch. I am sure that he, along with other members of the committee, would be among the first to admit that many of the achievements of the branch during the last few years have resulted directly from the policies of the former government. A number of firsts came into being in the last five years, not the least of which was the granting of the franchise to the Indian people of Canada. As Canadians generally know, this was done by the former government.
However, I want to bring out this point specifically because the minister, in speaking on citizenship in general in Canada, referred to the relation of citizenship to the Indian people and stated, as we all do from time to time, that he was looking forward to the day when they will become full-fledged citizens of our country. I am sure there is general agreement that the granting of the franchise to the Indians, giving them the right to vote in federal elections, was a big step toward their becoming the equals of everyone else in Canada.
A number of other things were done by the previous government, such as the setting up of the very important joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs. The deliberations of this committee took some months and extended over the better part of three years. I am sure the many reports of that committee are going to be of considerable benefit to the officials of the Indian affairs branch and to people in general who are interested in bringing about a better way of life for our Indian people.
I think it will also be agreed that the subject of our Indians is one of the most important, if not the most important, internal matter that we have before us in Canada at the present time. Granted that such things as trade and other subjects are of high priority, the problem of establishing a better way of life for the Indian people is one which we must consider of primary importance. I say this particularly in view of the expanding Indian population. I do not have the figures for the total Indian population of Canada, but I would venture a guess that it must be somewhere in the neighbourhood of 170,000 or 200,000. This is
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration just a figure I have pulled out of the air. I do know that the Indian population in the constituency which I have the honour to represent is increasing very rapidly. Figures were given to me in January, 1962 indicating that the Indian population of Churchill constituency was around 9,383. In October, 1963, the population had increased to 10,621. We have therefore, an increase of 1,238 in a little over 15 months.
There are 17 Indian reservations in the northern part of Manitoba and all 17 are in the Churchill constituency. I can assure you, therefore, that we in northern Manitoba realize the importance of this problem. We realize it is not one which is going to be easily resolved. I must admit that the educational facilities are available. The necessity for more and more educational facilities is also of primary importance. As we have all heard many times education, in itself, is not going to be the solution. However education, coupled with other measures, is a definite requirement. In that respect, it is gratifying to know that today practically all Indian children of school age in Canada have facilities of one kind or another available to them to enable them to receive an education. It is gratifying also to know that practically every Indian student who wishes to continue into the field of higher education also has facilities available to him.
As I say, the giant strides which have been taken to provide these greatly needed educational facilities are not, in themselves, going to be the solution. We hear a great deal of public criticism directed against the Indian people. We hear that they are shiftless, that they are lazy and will not try to help themselves. We hear that, when given an opportunity to work, they have a record of poor attendance on the job. This is one of the prime topics of conversation amongst white people when they get together in groups to try to see what can be done to better the situation of the Indian people. I am sure anyone who has had the opportunity of visiting these people, particularly the ones living on reservations in more isolated areas, will find all kinds of people there, just as you will find all kinds of people when you visit a white community. The vast majority of the Indian people, with whom I have come in contact in northern Manitoba, have every desire to better themselves. The main request which the chiefs and the councils make every time you meet with them is the need for employment.
As I said, we hear many people in Canada say that the Indian people are not interested in working. I can assure you that in the main, this is far from the truth. If it were possible, all we need to do is put ourselves in the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration position in which we have put the Indians, and then see just what sort of a transformation the white people would make if they were obliged to live under the same conditions as some of these Indian people live on these reservations. I am sure the people in the Indian affairs branch realize that many of these Indians have to go anywhere from a quarter of a mile to a greater distance than that to get water. It is true that many of the reservations, particularly in the north, are located on the shores of lakes and that most of the dwellings are close to those lakes. However, in many cases there are no dock facilities and the banks of the lakes are steep and rocky. When a woman or a small child is obliged to go for water, it is found that the most convenient place to get that water is sometimes more than a quarter of a mile away.
As I have said, I should like to see a test made to ascertain how some of the white people would fare if they lived under the same conditions as the Indians. I often wonder what their health situation would be, what the standard of cleanliness in a house would be, and other things. These are not the only things that confront people living on reservations. Many people say, why don't they raise a good deal of their own produce? I will admit that many projects have been carried out by the officials of the Indian affairs branch to try to get some of these people to have their own gardens and harvest the produce at the end of the season.
If you were to travel through northern Manitoba, and I imagine it is the same in most of the other areas, you would find a great many of these reserves are in areas where the land is far from arable. It is almost impossible, even with a tremendous amount of work, for more than one or two people to have small gardens. We hear this criticism of the Indian people from a lot of people who have not had the opportunity, or who have not taken the time to visit them. These white people take many things for granted and more or less write off the Indians because they say if the Indians will not help themselves there is no obligation on the rest of the people in Canada to do very much about them. Some people say that the Indians use some very queer methods in their attempts to live on the land.
For instance, we often hear it said by white people that the Indian will never cut enough wood to last for more than one day. This is quite true in a good many cases. However, there is a free trader on one reserve I visit who has adopted a plan to solve this problem. When I explain it to some of the people they say, well this is the most foolish thing I ever heard so far as the Indians are


concerned. I should like to give you an example of how this plan works, and to say that the Indians have their own reasons for doing these things.
This man has adopted the idea of letting these fellows go out in July and August to cut 10 or 15 cords of wood, which they haul in and pile beside his store. He then pays them $6 a cord for it and they go away quite happy. When the trapping season comes around the Indians get a little more money and they save it until January or February, when they go back to the storekeeper and buy the wood from him at $9 a cord.
Most people ask why they do not cut the wood and haul it to their own cabins and so save $3 a cord. The reason is that in summer time these people need the $6 that they get, and during the trapping season they can afford to buy the wood back at a little more than they were paid for it. This is the kind of thing which makes white people say the Indian is a foolish person; but if we were to tell the Indian people about some of the tragedies white people get themselves into by taking too much advantage of credit systems, I wonder what the Indians would think of white people.
Generally speaking the Indian affairs branch has a large number of very capable personnel, including field men, agents, assistant agents and so on. But when a visitor goes to an Indian reservation he generally hears complaints against the agent. In the main these complaints are not justified. In many cases the agent just does not have the knack of gaining the confidence of the Indian people. When this happens, and when a series of complaints come in, the department should take a good look at the official in charge, and instead of moving him to some other area should call him in for a good talk, possibly provide him with some kind of refresher course, and impress upon him the necessity of gaining the confidence of these people and co-operating with them.
In northern Manitoba the personnel of the Indian affairs branch are dedicated people doing a very good job, but we do have complaints. Some people feel the agents need more instruction and a little more experience before they are put into these positions. Many of the areas need more field men. Usually an agent has a large territory to cover, and on top of that he has numerous reports to write. Therefore he does not have the time to cover the area properly and keep in constant touch with the Indian reservations which he administers.
This year at Thompson, Manitoba, a work project was undertaken in the Nelson House area in conjunction with the community development work of the province. The Indian

affairs branch put a dedicated man in there to try and re-arrange the trap lines and assist the Indians to achieve a better way of Ashing. Certain lakes were selected. Ice houses were built, and an overseer was installed to see that the Ashing was done in a better manner for the beneAt of the Indians. Several trap lines were re-arranged, and where capable trappers were not manning them, other Indians were put in charge, and things were improving greatly.
However, the main trouble was that the money allocated for the work was insufficient. The man in charge found he had to spend most of his time at Thompson because there was not enough money to enable him to travel to the lakes where he had these projects set up; and if he travelled to the lakes, the reports he was expected to send periodically to the branch were not going in, and complaints were coming from the head office. It was a case of one man, who was supposed to be in three different places at one time, trying to carry out a very worthwhile project; and if some changes are not made this project will go overboard. Having inspected it myself I can assure the committee it could do a great deal of good for that particular community.
One of the biggest problems is the lack of employment for Indians. This is understandable because mainly they are in isolated places where the only employment is self-employment, trapping and Ashing during the respective seasons. Unless there is a little bit of brush clearing for a winter road constructed by a province, or some small work arranged by the branch on a reserve, there is no employment whatsoever for the balance of the year.
In the case of many reserves there are small lumber mills, possibly several hundred miles away, and work projects such as northern roads being built under contract. Generally, however, the people in charge of a contract or operating small saw mills are very reluctant to hire Indians. Now, the government is claiming a great deal of credit for its new program which provides Anancial assistance to employers who employ older workers. Possibly the same project could be undertaken by the Indian affairs branch in co-operation with the Department of Labour, to give some encouragement to these contractors and saw mill operators to hire Indian labour.
I realize my time is running out but, Mr. Chairman, I would like to see particular attention given to the formation of a separate department of Indian affairs. This is one of the most important problems we have, and it is becoming rapidly greater as the population increases. If we do not tackle it much more
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration quickly than we are doing, then in 20 or 25 years it will be that much harder to deal with. Therefore consideration should be given to the formation of a separate department and, if not a separate department at least a special deputy minister who would do nothing but look after the Indian affairs branch.
As I said before, I would also like to see consideration given towards providing more Aeld personnel in the outlying areas. There is a lot of work that can be done on reservations in the Aeld of local improvements. Many suggestions along this line have been made to the Indian affairs branch, and it has been suggested that in lieu of paying out welfare, these men should be given some remuneration for doing drainage work, fencing, and other jobs on the reservations, such as a general clean up each year. In that way they could be paid instead of being handed welfare.
There may be immediate criticism of this. Some may say it would be setting a precedent. I do not think it would be setting a precedent at all, because I understand that in many of our cities where the city is handling relief measures, if they get a heavy snowfall or something like that, the able-bodied men who are on relief-they have a list of such people-are immediately put to work on snow removal. If they will not do this work of snow removal, they are taken off the relief roll. I think this could be adopted very easily by the Indian affairs branch in regard to improvement work being done on the Indian reservations. The Indians themselves could do the work and be paid for it, in lieu of welfare payments.
Carried.

I have a few more things to say, Mr. Chairman. I think some consideration should also be given to small Anancial assistance being provided to the chiefs and councillors of various bands. I do not think they should be given any great remuneration, and I realize they have band funds out of which the bands themselves can appropriate money. Chiefs and councillors attend a number of meetings each year, and many of these bands do not have a great deal of funds to their credit. Some of these chiefs and councillors have to do a considerable amount of travelling. For instance, in the Island Lake reserve in Manitoba there is one chief and his councillors, but the band is split into two separate communities which are approximately seven or eight miles apart; they have nothing but seven or eight miles of water between them. This means there is a considerable amount of going back and forth between the two different communities by the chief and councillors. Under present conditions the remuneration they receive does

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration not cover the cost of this travelling, which is necessary to look after the needs of their people.
There is one final thing I should like to mention. With regard to a long term look at this picture and what can be done for these people, I would like the government to consider sponsoring a course of some kind in some of our universities, or at least in one of our universities. This should be a course for students to specialize in renewable resources, particularly the betterment of the quality of our fur-bearing animals, improvement in the methods of fishing, improvement in the methods of not only the harvesting of wild rice but in encouraging the growing of wild rice in larger areas. If some such course were available in the universities, graduates of that course could be hired by the Indian affairs branch and sent into the Indian communities. These people could give considerable assistance to the Indian people, not only in the trapping of animals but in the handling of the pelts and, of course, in better methods of fishing. I can envision, for instance, one good graduate taking eight or ten Indian families and making them selfsufficient all the year round, if they were put into good trapping and fishing areas. These people could also instruct the Indian people in the art of being capable and competent tourist guides during the fishing and hunting seasons. In that respect-

Mr. Chairman, I should like to address a few remarks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, particularly related to the management of Indian affairs in this country. The announcement that there will be a further slight delay in the setting up of the Indian claims commission I greet with some regret, even though I know it will certainly be done very soon. I am thinking of the convention of the national Indian council in Winnipeg, Manitoba, which the minister and myself attended, at which he assured the Indian people who were at the meeting from all across this country that this commission would be active before Christmas. I know the minister meant this. I also know that the Indian people who were at that meeting believed him. I merely want to say that in my country the person who says something and does not do it, regardless of the reason, is labelled as one who "speaks with a crooked tongue". I would like to suggest to the minister-in fact, I am going to insist that the minister and his officials notify those Indian people who came from all parts of Canada that there will be this further


delay. If he does that, he will have the reputation of a man who speaks with a straight tongue.
I believe that most Canadian citizens have a vague feeling of smugness in believing our treatment of the Canadian Indian has on the whole been quite humane. In fact, however, there have been some examples in our development which, although they are not generally known-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I do not wish to have it on record that any Indian in this country may even have occasion to say that their superintendent general has spoken with a crooked tongue. I have never said-and hon. members in this house can confirm this, those who have read the reports of my speech in Winnipeg will confirm it, and my speech will confirm it-that the Indian claims commission would be put to work before the end of 1963. What I said, and what I promised, after consultation with the Prime Minister, was that legislation would be introduced before the end of this year, with the intention of providing for the establishment of an Indian claims commission. I hope my hon. friend who has just made the statement will try to recall what he heard in Winnipeg and will correct the record in consequence, because the words he has uttered are an accusation which, as far as I am concerned, I am not ready to admit or accept.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to put on the record that the belief of the people, after hearing the minister, whom they believed, and whom I believe, was that in fact some work would be done by the commission before the end of this year. I will certainly state for the record that I withdraw any suggestion the minister may feel I made that he was attempting to deceive these people. I believe quite to the contrary. My suggestion to him was that if there was to be a further delay-and there will be-let those Indian people know of the further delay, not just the members of this house; and let them know the new date on which in fact the commission will be at work. If the minister does that he will retain the trust the Indian people have in him right now, and I can assure him from my meetings with the delegates at the convention that they do trust him. My suggestion was made in a spirit of friendliness and co-operation, and I certainly did not want to suggest that I was accusing the minister of anything.
I was stating that Canadians generally tend to feel pretty smug about how humane we

have been, but there have been some unfortunate examples of treatment toward Indians. You have only to think of the Beothuk Indians who lived in Newfoundland, true at a time when that part of the country was not in Canada, who were over a period of some 200 years purposely exterminated by the white settlers in that part of the country. Furthermore, there are many ways in which to destroy a race of people. Hunger, cold, tuberculosis and syphilis will destroy a race as surely as bullets.
When the Glassco commission examined management of Indian affairs in the Northwest Territories they recommended that services to the Indians be integrated. They further recommended that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in effect administer the affairs of all Indian people. Personally I disagree with this, and I wish the minister to be aware that I think there is no point in turning over the administration of the affairs of a group of people from one federal agency to another. Furthermore, with the extensive workload that the officials of northern affairs already have cut out for them in the Northwest Territories, I do not think they can handle it as well as does the Indian Affairs branch now. If the suggestion is at any time made that Indian affairs work in the Northwest Territories be handled by the territorial government of the Northwest Territories, and if within a year or two the government of the Northwest Territories is in fact elected by the people, I would be the first to support the idea that Indian affairs be handled by that agency.
In the meantime I think it is most important that the Indian affairs branch in the Northwest Territories revise their programs of assistance so as to bring them up to the level of assistance received by the Eskimo, the white and the Metis people who are in identical circumstances. At the present time we have several communities in which these three "administrative" groups live side by side. An Indian widow on relief with, let us say, four children, receives in welfare assistance substantially less than a widow with four children who is not an Indian. This creates friction and misunderstanding and confounds the officials of the department who are trying to do a good job. So that even though the day when we can integrate services to Indians in the Northwest Territories may be several years off, I beg the minister in the meantime at least to see to it that the scales of assistance and programs provided Indian people are as generous and as good as those offered to non-Indians.
I also want to bring to the minister's attention treaties Nos. 8 and 11. It is not gen-
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration erally known in Canada that the Canadian government has never lived up to the two major terms in those treaties. While the bulk of the Indian people are quite happy not to be put on reserves or to have their homes built on reserves, they are unhappy because the reason for this is that the Canadian government has never lived up to its treaty commitments.
The original treaty signed by these people said that we shall provide for every five Indians one square mile of land. This has never been done. In 1957 the Indian chiefs met. They know that this land has never been given to them. They met in Fort Smith and discussed this matter, and the Indian affairs branch officials assured them that something would be done. In 1959 a royal commission was set up to examine the unfulfilled provisions of treaties Nos. 8 and 11. This royal commission made an extensive study, interviewed Indian people, and made recommendations. These recommendations were referred to the Indian affairs branch for action. The other major benefit which we promised the Indian people in these two treaties has also not been lived up to, and it is a source of concern all over Canada. They-

Go back to the Indian bands and renegotiate these treaties. They are not sacred. They cannot be sacred, because the Canadian government has never lived up to the provisions of them, anyway. Go back to the Indians and point out to them the conservation needs of the country. Indian people can understand these things, if they can trust those who are going to sign the treaty. I guarantee the Indians will sit down in good faith, bargain with him and renegotiate the whole position, because this is a matter as it now stands that only leads to a feeling on the part of the Indian people that they cannot trust any white man or government official.
I suggest that in many instances we are asking the Indian people to carry on as though we were in the middle of the 18th century. Everything we have done to develop the country has militated against the ability of the Indian people to live on the land. We have put in schools and impressed on the Indian people the importance of sending children to school every day. We cannot then turn around and say to them: Take your wife and the pre-school children and leave the settlement. Our missionaries have introduced a new religion. They have said: Go to church regularly; get married in church before you start raising your children. This militates against a life on the land because the churches are located in settlements. We have gone to the people and said: At the first sign of a cold, bring your children into the nursing station; don't get your feet wet; avoid extremes of weather. On the other hand we say: Why aren't you out trapping in the bush, miles away from all these services which we have told you are good.
We have to start giving the Indians more than advice. There is a saying in my country which goes like this: You cannot make soup out of caribou tracks. The Indian people need more than words; they need our technology. When I think of the kind of thing that is being done in other countries to help local people harvest their resources-and the hon. member for Churchill referred to this point-I am reminded of some of the things the Russians have done, if you will pardon the expression, in the harvesting of fish. They pump fish. They have ships with pumps that work like a vacuum cleaner. They use radar to locate the fish, and then they suck

them in. When I hear that, and when I hear of an Indian agent along the Mackenzie river giving a man a three and a half inch net and telling him to go out and make a good living for himself and his family, I say it is time we got some new ideas in dealing with the Indian people and made available, not just our school facilities and health services but our 20th century technology.
Words are not enough. There are suggestions made regularly, not overtly, but none the less they are made, that the Indian people of Canada are second class citizens. Let me say this: They are second class citizens, but not because they are Indians. They are second class because anyone who is cold, hungry, unemployed and uneducated, any group of people who are weakened and despised and dispersed are second class. If you want to do something about this we shall give them an opportunity to take advantage of the technology we now have, to give them a little opportunity to be first class citizens.
In conclusion, let me say this: I should like to see the minister set for himself a plan which would exterminate this whole branch within a set time. The period I would like to suggest is a 20 year period-the great leap into oblivion-during which he should devote all the efforts of his department to making sure that the branch does not exist 20 years from now. I say 20 years, because this would give time for all the people who have careers in the branch to be retired. They would not be threatened. And all the new ones who come in could be told that there was a limited period in which they would be required to work. I am afraid, when I learn there are more Indians being born each year than either die or become enfranchised; because I see in this situation only the possibility of the Indian affairs branch continuing to grow and the Indian people always being controlled by a special department set up for them.
I know many of the minister's officials are working with the province now to see that health, education and welfare services are taken over by provincial authorities. I urge the minister to give his officials who are doing these things every encouragement, so that when he presents his estimates again-and I trust it is the same minister who is presenting them at this time, because I have confidence in him and his ideas-he may be able to include in them some kind of plan which will in the long run eliminate the need for his department altogether.

unanimous consent to the passage of the resolution, to grant it so that the bill can be introduced. I think every member in this party is of the same opinion. The minister made reference to a variety of activities of the department in the field of welfare, sewerage, water systems, education and the like. I do not believe it is necessary to comment specifically on them, except to say that I know of particular bands who have been somewhat miffed in years past by the activities of the Indian affairs branch in connection with water and sewerage systems. I certainly would not want to see repeated the experience which some bands have had. I know of one band in particular, right offhand I could not tell you the name, which has spent hundreds of dollars on a water system over a period of years in an attempt to make it efficient and effective. The reason for spending the additional amount of money is that when the water system was constructed in the first instance, the engineers or whoever was responsible for the installation, put the pipes in backwards. They put the small pipes at the source of the water supply and down near the houses they put the larger pipes, which is the reverse of what should have been done.
There is another Indian village on the coast, I do not want to mention the name of it, in which over a period of years some $30,000 has been spent in an attempt to instal a water supply system for the people. They have a beautiful looking water tank sitting up on top of a hill some distance behind the village and close to a creek upon which a dam was constructed. Perhaps more than $30,000 has been spent on this water system over a period of years, but not a single drop of water has come through the system. We do not want to see these things repeated, and I am sure the Indian people do not either. I do not want to go into specific cases, but I am sure that if the minister just asks for a review by his officers he will find that the two incidents to which I have referred were not isolated incidents. These conditions have existed for a long time in the operations of the Indian affairs branch.
The minister phrased his introductory remarks in fine language. I have read a number of press releases of speeches the minister made outside the house, and on every occasion these statements were phrased in fine words.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I do not wish to be unkind to him, but words are cheap, statements are easy to prepare, especially if one is learned in the language or learned in the law. Especially in view of the experience the native people have had in trying to solve their problems over the years, speeches, phrases and words must be backed up by action before the people will believe the minister. This is what we are waiting for, this is what we are looking forward to seeing.
At different times, I have had occasion to read the speeches made in this house by the minister's various predecessors. The Hon. Walter Harris, when he was minister, used to make some fine speeches. The present Secretary of State, when he held the post of minister of citizenship and immigration, spoke highly and emotionally about Indian affairs and the things that should be done for the Indian people. Incidentally, he spoke even more emotionally about those things when he sat in opposition. Nevertheless, his speeches make fine reading. Even the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Mrs. Fair-clough, spoke nicely about Indian affairs. However, over the years, the actions that have emanated from the government have not met the expectations which the Indian people had as a result of these statements and speeches.
The native Indian people want to see some action. They are trusting people. They are fine, upstanding citizens of this nation and they should be recognized. I hope that action will be forthcoming, and when it does that it will meet the expectations of the people of this nation, especially in view of the great amount of the milk of human kindness that is contained in the speeches of the various ministers, including the present one. Unfortunately, I believe the fathers of confederation made a mistake in the British North America Act in confining the jurisdiction over Indians and lands reserved for Indians to the parliament of Canada. In one sense, this casts some doubt upon the legality of the various dominion-provincial programs that are in existence, especially those co-operative programs on education that have been increasing over the years. There is some doubt expressed as to whether the parliament of Canada is able to delegate its authority in this field because of the provisions of the British North America Act, but I do not want to cast doubt upon that because I think this is the course of action we should be following-that is, getting out of the business of Indian affairs and getting it into the hands of the provincial governments where the civil and other rights of our other citizens rest, and where the civil and other rights of the Indian people should rest.
So long as we have an Indian affairs branch, and that provision in the British

North America Act, we are going to have two classes of people, one the native Indians who come under the jurisdiction of this parliament, and the other encompassing everybody else, whose jurisdiction is within the hands of the provinces. So long as we have a separate law on the statute books of Canada revolving around a group of people because of their racial background, it is going to beget discrimination in one form or another.
The mere fact that there is a separate law governing Indians makes people ask themselves whether the people covered by that law are different? If we had a separate act on the statute books covering the French people, and called the French act, people would say there must be something queer about the French. If we had a separate law relating to Scotch people, called the Scotch act, other people would say there must be something rather weird about the Scotch. I know many people have these opinions anyway, but if we had laws to such effect they would promote discrimination, in the same way as the very fact that we have an Indian Act does.
Unfortunately, no matter how much one may hope that the Indian affairs branch will have the initiative and momentum within it to be able to solve these problems, I do not think it can. To me the Indian affairs branch is an administrative organization. It is concerned with the keeping of files and records, the writing of letters and the preparation of documents. It does not concern itself with, and in fact it is impossible for it to be concerned with anything other than administration. It does not get into the field of developing policy, although there are some people who say it does; and it cannot get into the field of sociological research, and the like.
Accordingly, because it is bound by its own red tape and its own pyramidal structure, it is unable to do anything other than administer. It is a sort of conglomeration of office managers, and this does not help the problem of Indian affairs.
At one time the law used to refer to the individual in the field as the Indian agent, the implication being he was an agent of the Indian people. This was the concept of his original appointment, that he would be an agent to act on behalf of the Indian people in dealing with governments and other elements of society. Now the law has been changed. He is an Indian superintendent, and the very word superintendent carries with it the connotation of a supervisor, foreman, or boss of some sort. The minister himself has got an even higher faluting title: He is the superintendent general, a sort of super foreman over everybody else. This is precisely the attitude many superintendents have that

they are there to supervise the Indian people in their daily life, to represent the administrative machinery, and that they are not there to help the Indian people themselves.
Because of all these factors, and regardless of how much one may admire individuals in the Indian affairs branch, regardless of how much their hearts may be set on accomplishing something worth while, and no matter how fine an understanding individuals may have in the Indian affairs branch, they cannot give full effect to their feelings. The branch, by its very existence and structure, is an incompetent organization to deal fully and completely with the various problems confronting Indian people, problems that have developed over the last 100 years and which started some time before that.
To a great extent the branch is a narrow neck funnel through which ideas eventually filter to the minister. The minister's predecessors were not too interested in trying to break out of these bonds, and in trying to establish something different. I hope the minister is interested in this.
Unfortunately the Indian people look to the Indian affairs branch from the point of view as expressed to them by the political head of that department, whoever the minister may happen to be. To them the minister, being a representative of Her Majesty in the old traditional sense, because their treaties were phrased that way, they look upon him as being the sole guiding light in Indian affairs. But because we have had a succession of changes of ministers we have a confused attitude both in administration and in the approach by native Indian people to the government's tackling of Indian affairs. This is partly because the fine phrases, to which I referred earlier, have not been carried out and formulated into action, and this has largely been due to the succession of changes of ministers.
I would rather that the minister would not accept the contention of the hon. member for Churchill and others to the effect that we need a separate department of Indian affairs, or that the chief director of Indian affairs should be a deputy minister and given more authority and power within the structure of government; and I say this because our goal and objective must be repeal of the Indian Act, must be the transfer of the jurisdiction of various activities of the branch to the provincial governments, and this at a speed to meet the desires of the Indian people, and not to be foisted upon them.
We will not be able to proceed in that direction if we proceed in the direction of building an empire around the minister in the government. If we establish a separate department of Indian affairs we will bring into
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration being a group of empire builders and make it more difficult for the federal government to get out of the field of Indian affairs.
What I would like to see is that the government take steps to establish a board, commission or council-it does not matter what you call it-for the economic advancement of native peoples, a body that will be free from interference in its activities by the Indian affairs branch. It should be a body that will be free from political and ministerial influence in its day to day activities; which will have on it people who are native Indians representing the native points of view; which will have on it people schooled in the fields of sociology and anthropology, people well versed in the field of education-economists, representatives of the professions and the like -and this body should have as its guide posts the promotion of a variety of activities which the Indian affairs branch now conducts, or attempts to conduct, in the field of economic development activity.
Such a body should have a program of job opportunities and job placements within its sphere of activities. It should embrace the field of adult education, and the all important field of band council education, in an attempt to prompt band councils to become masters of their own destinies, rather than what they now are, minions of the Indian agent in whatever the agent can get away with. This body should have as its eventual goal an approach to working with the economic councils that exist in Canada, the various economic boards in the provinces and other agencies, with the hope of transferring as much of this activity as possible to the provincial governments, again at a speed which meets the desires of the Indian people.
We could then confine the activities of the Indian affairs branch to that which it knows best and does the most effectively, namely the dispensing of welfare or assistance of that sort, with the goal being to transfer these jurisdictions to the provincial governments, again at a speed which meets the desires of the native peoples themselves.
When it comes to the question of welfare I would like to make this comment. The amount payable now, in general terms, is $22 per month. This was established in 1957 or 1958, I believe, and replaced the old ration system of welfare assistance. This compares, again in pretty general terms, with welfare assistance payable in the province of British Columbia of $66 a month. So if you are an Indian, you get $22; if you are a non-Indian or an Indian living off the reserve, you are likely to get $66. We would like to see some sort of uniformity in this assistance, because

While on this particular subject, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make reference to an agreement which was consummated the first part of this year between the federal government and the government of British Columbia. It was implemented on January 1, as a matter of fact. It is covered in what is called a statement of policy on social assistance and health services to Indians in British Columbia. So, even in this enlightened year of 1963 this is what the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia agreed to do with respect to welfare. They agreed to put into writing and permit a continuation of a system of paying welfare based on discrimination, based on racial origin, based on whether a person is an Indian or is not an Indian, and based upon whether a person lives on or off a reserve, which makes it even worse. What happens under that agreement? I do not think it is necessary to read it entirely into the record, but it says that an Indian who has lived continuously without social assistance directly from a municipal, provincial or federal government for one year off the reserve is the responsibility of the local area.
So if an Indian lives off the reserve for one year he is entitled, if he needs welfare, to receive welfare amounts from the provincial government; but if he lives on the reserve, what happens to him-he receives the $22 a month. Surely to heaven in the first part of this year, when we were talking about transfer of jurisdiction and equality, it would have been sensible for the government to have attempted to put into effect a system in the province of British Columbia which would be based upon equality of treatment for native people and do away with the old system of discrimination. As far as I am concerned, this system is also a bloody disgrace, if I can use that word, to this parliament and to the government of British Columbia; and it is a disgrace to all those people in Canada who allowed it to happen. I hope this government will take steps to have it repealed or changed, because after all, what difference is there between one person and another when it comes to his needs and requirements in order to keep body and soul together?
I think the mere word "integration" is a curse to the Indian people. "Integration" carries with it some very bad connotations, because it means and has meant in the past to many officials in government, a one way street. "Integration" means to the Indian people, "You give up your heritage, your culture, your language and your background. You give up what you know about your


people's ancestors and how they lived in this nation, and you come into our way of living and accept everything that we have". To me this is not a sensible course to follow. What other word one can find, I do not know, unless it might be acculturation. But the approach in the relationship between Indian people and those of non-Indian origin must in all instances be based on mutual respect, mutual understanding, mutual trust and confidence and upon attempting to promote equality in all fields. It must be based on the desire of the non-Indian people-and this must emanate from government somewhere-to understand and respect the background of the arts that native people have. Incidentally, the only truly North American art form that has ever been developed is that of the totemic carving of the Indians along the west coast.
One must understand and have a desire to appreciate the participation of native people in the field of politics. One has only to read or talk with people who know about the Iroquois nation to appreciate what a remarkably fine political system and structure they have. It is one which would be well for us to copy and put parts of it into effect. We must attempt to understand and appreciate more the intense hereditary feeling of cooperation that exists amongst native people, because they far excel us in the field of co-operating and working together for the mutual benefit of all. In the past our forefathers destroyed the economic base of Indian native people. They did not do a single, solitary thing to replace it with anything else or attempt to train native people to fit into any other type of economy. Unfortunately, many of the missionaries in fact-although they did not realize they were doing this- destroyed to a great extent the religious base of native Indian people and replaced it with something which at that time was alien to them.
For all these reasons, together with a variety of others, the native Indian person has come, as the hon. member from the Northwest Territories said, to distrust practically every single thing that the non-Indian person, especially government and the Indian affairs branch, does. As I said earlier in my opening remarks, it will take more than fine phrases, it will take more than fine words, it will take more than long statements by the minister to counteract this distrust. It will take a long series of actions in a trustworthy way, carried out fully, before the native people will trust us as we should desire to trust and respect them.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if I could close by reading the attitude developed by the New Democratic party convention with regard to Indian affairs. Incidentally, ours is the only

political party in existence which in open convention developed a concept about native Indian affairs. We say this:
The New Democratic party has as a basic philosophy the recognition of the dignity of the human being; a respect for moral and cultural values; a belief in equality without regard to race, creed, colour, or religion; a deep desire to foster mutual trust and respect among all peoples; the will to promote advancements in the spheres of education, peace, security and freedom-
I know that the native Indian of Canada has in the past had his needs and hopes disregarded and sacrificed. Based on those words, we in the New Democratic party fervently hope that this parliament, this government, will find a way to solve the problems confronting our native Indian people and so assist all of us to reach a higher plane of dignity and work in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to discuss matters of citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs. My first remarks must be addressed to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and what follows will be addressed to the superintendent general of Indian affairs. I must say that I am very thankful for the cooperation the minister and his able and cooperative young parliamentary secretary have shown in any of the dealings I have had with them. I do hope the minister realizes this is one of the most important portfolios in the government of Canada, and I hope that a man who has shown the interest he has shown in that department is not removed and somebody else put in his place, as has been mentioned in news items in various newspapers. It would be a travesty of justice, decency, and everything else were he to be removed and the person mentioned put in his place. My interest in citizenship and immigration is very great because I represent the constituency of Vegreville, in Alberta, which is populated by people from perhaps 40 different nations. This getting together of so many people from different nations has resulted in intermarriage; and we now have one culture and we are Canadians there. Yet there are still difficulties with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
I should just like to mention three different types of situation, cases which I have picked out from my filing cabinets, concerning communications which have been carried on with the minister. The first one was brought to my attention by a man a little younger than I who was born in the same district as I was. His people came from Poland. By the time the last war had ended he had become fairly well provided with worldly goods, and he had a niece in Poland whom he wanted
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to bring to Canada. This girl was aged 20 years, although she is probably 22 now because this case commenced two or three years ago. This man has been refused permission to bring his niece to this country because he is not closely enough related. He has guaranteed to see that she never becomes a charge on the state. She is his niece, a daughter of his sister who was killed in the war. In fact her whole family was killed; she is the only one left. Yet this man cannot bring her to this country. These people, who are Canadians, have asked me as well as other members of parliament to help them, but we were not able to do anything for them. I think cases like this should get priority. There is not a chance in the world of this girl's becoming a charge on the state; and the people who want to bring her to the country are some of our best citizens.
I now go to the case of a Ukrainian girl born somewhere in the Ukraine. Both the minister and his parliamentary secretary know this case very well because I have a very thick file on it. This girl came to Canada in 1939 when she was between three and six years of age. In 1955 her mother, her father and her sister as well as 'she herself applied for Canadian citizenship. The mother got her citizenship but the father and the two daughters were refused. I have been working on this case for only about a year, and during that time I have discussed it with two ministers of citizenship, both of whom have been very interested; but because of certain reports gathered together, I presume by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, there is very great difficulty in this young lady's getting her Canadian citizenship.
This girl I am talking about is a bachelor of education from the University of Alberta. She has been a high school teacher for the last ten years, and her sister to whom I referred is a registered nurse, but she has now married a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and has received her citizenship. Why in the name of heaven can this girl, who is a couple of years older than her sister, not get her citizenship? I know there is a private file not available to people as far down the ladder as I am, but I think there must have been some error in the reports which were accumulated and gathered by the R.C.M.P. and turned over to the department of citizenship. I may say that the judge in the citizenship court in the city of Edmonton has, I am told, recommended each time that she has applied that this girl be given citizenship. We will have to smarten up and do something about cases like this. I say that we should have a judicial committee appointed which sits all the time to handle appeals from decisions like this; and this

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration committee should be appointed forthwith. I am sorry I cannot go into these cases in too much detail because I am restricted as to time.
My third case concerns a man who came to this country from England. He did not come here direct; he came to the United States in 1950. He served with the British army, starting out as a private soldier during the last war. He was a commando, became a major and was decorated by the King with the military cross for conspicuous gallantry. This man came to Canada, as I say, through the United States in 1956, I believe it was. When he went to the United States in 1950 he had a British passport. When he came to Canada in 1956 the customs inspector at the point of entry did not stamp his passport. No record was taken of his entry. In 1958 he went back to England, and landed back in Gander, Newfoundland, coming through the Canadian customs at Gander. He was still carrying his British passport and it was marked with a stamp authorizing re-entry into Canada. This man wants his Canadian citizenship. He has been here seven years, so why in the name of heaven are so many difficulties put in his way?
These are only a few of the vast number of cases I have of this sort, and due to shortness of time I do not want to go into any of them too fully. I did remark that I thought there should be a judicial committee authorized to hear complaints against refusals to grant citizenship, and I know the minister and his assistants are doing everything they can. I am not complaining against that. I am complaining about the Canadian Citizenship Act and the fact that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has to be so darn stuffy about allowing people to become Canadians.
Now I wish to address the next part of my few remarks to the superintendent general of Indian affairs. May I remark first to him that I am very pleased to notice on today's order paper the fact that he has at last got around to providing for the establishment an Indian claims commission, to providing for the duties of the commission, its decision and awards, and to providing for appeals from the decisions of the commission to the Indian claims appeal court, and to enact such financial provisions as may be necessary to accomplish the purposes of the act.
I assure you that that is something I have advocated for a long time. The Conservative party has advocated that, but it was not possible to bring it into being. Had we been returned as the government this would have been brought in; if not earlier than this, it would have been brought in by now, anyway. I must say that when I speak of Indian


affairs I am talking from experience, because when I was born out in the place in which I still live, our closest neighbours were Indians. Therefore I speak with experience when I speak of Indian affairs. As I have said so many times already, I regret that my time does not allow me to go into it fully but if the minister and his assistants wish to hear the whole story they can take a week off some time, and I will, too, and I will give them an earful.
The reserve I am most interested in at the moment is the Saddle Lake reserve, which is part of the Saddle Lake agency. This agency comprises some six or seven bands of Indians. The rest of the bands under the control of that agency are in the constituency of the hon. member for Athabasca. The same difficulties beset my Indians as beset his. In this Saddle Lake Indian reserve in my constituency there are between 1,200 and 1,300 Indians. I want to say that they are on the whole a very progressive people. As everybody should know, there is nothing the matter with the Indians for which the white man has not been responsible. There are a few of them of course, as in every race, who are shiftless but on the whole they are very industrious.
I may say that the Liberal opposition candidate in my constituency who ran against me was a treaty Indian on my reserve. He got his first vote, and do you know, we gave it to him, and he ran as a Liberal. We made it possible, and he became a Liberal candidate and he is a very-
Be careful.

He is a very able man. But I am not out campaigning for him now because he is on some royal commission or something, I guess it was the Postmaster General who got his name. I am telling the committee this to show that the Indians can take their place alongside anybody, make no mistake about that. These people were the first Canadians and, really, they are the only Canadians. The rest of us are all immigrants. They have had a thin time since the white man came and took their country away from them. I know that out west the story only goes back as far as 1885 or 1889, some 80 years ago. Anyway, they were herded on to reserves. They did not get very much opportunity to progress. Only now are they beginning to come into their own and they are now, as I do not need to tell anybody here, a very vocal part of the Canadian population. They want to make up for the things they have been denied throughout all these years, and they will certainly be able to speak for themselves when they come before this Indian

claims commission or any other commission to which they may have access.
There are several things I should like to mention and I am very happy that I helped to accomplish some of them. The two things I am going to mention first happened before the present minister took over this portfolio, that is, that the superintendent of the Saddle Lake agency is a fully blooded treaty Indian, which is a step in the right direction. If the Indians can rise to positions like that, they can help look after themselves, because a great many of the agents who have already been appointed in the past were civil servants and did not know much about the Indians. I do not know how some of them got into positions like that. But the agent there is doing an outstanding job. He is, as I said, a treaty Indian himself and he understands the difficulties with which these people are faced. That is one thing that was accomplished before the last election and since the 1962 election. There has also been medical supervision. There is a nurse on duty at all times on this reserve, now. Before she was established there, a nurse would be there for perhaps two hours on two days a week. It was a poor show, believe me, because people cannot organize their sicknesses to take place during the two hours a day on the two days of the week on which the nurse would be available.
One of the big complaints the Indians have is that their treaties have not been properly respected. They were made a long time ago, mostly, and the people who signed them on behalf of the Queen did not realize that western Canada particularly was going to reach the state of population it has now. They made deals about fishing and hunting. As the hon. member from the Northwest Territories remarked, if they shoot a duck out of season the R.C.M.P. are on their tail right away, and they are hauled into court. That is no part of any treaty ever made with them. With regard to fishing the situation is just about the same.
I realize that the federal government has turned over control of hunting and fishing to the provincial governments. This is something that should not have been done but I also appreciate that it perhaps became expedient to do it. In any event, these things worry the Indians a great deal, and it does not seem right that these people should be hauled into court for shooting a duck out of season. If they happen to come across a deer and shoot it a week before the official hunting season opens they are also hauled into court. If they fish in a lake where they are not supposed to fish, that is too bad, too. In any event, I will leave the matter there.
There is another matter that must be attended to, the provision of homes for the 28902-5-376
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration aged. I know these people get the old age pension but they have to live on it and cannot provide their own homes out of it. I realize that the minister wrote me a very sympathetic letter in which he said he was looking into the matter, but I want to emphasize that when the older Indians reach the age when they are no longer able to work they certainly need some place to live, and if they do not have a family to look after them they must find some place themselves. On the whole the accommodation provided for these old people on their reserves is no good at all.
The Indians are also not very happy because when the provincial government wants to put a road through their land they jolly well go ahead and do it. In some cases the provincial government has not made it stick, because in the case of the reserve in the constituency of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin I believe the Indians forced the provincial government to go around their reserve with the road.
The Indian Act should be reviewed again. I want to impress on the minister that whenever any changes are made in the Indian Act or in legislation which concerns the Indians these people must be consulted. They are very jealous of their rights and that is one right they should have. They say, and I agree with them, that nothing should be forced on them without their agreement.
The Indians are also troubled about the school situation. So far as the schools are concerned I am troubled about different things from what they are, but I will mention only what is troubling them. They are concerned about the fact that their children have to leave the reserve to go to school. They have to get up early in the morning to catch a bus and travel 25 or 35 miles to school. The bus is assigned to the reserve by the provincial government for this purpose. Some of the Indians think that the children are not ready for this. Some of the children go to a separate school and some go to the provincial Protestant school. Others are taken to schools closer to their homes but farther away from the main one in St. Paul. There are difficulties there, because in two of the towns to which these children are taken by bus there are only Protestant schools.
There is always trouble when the children of Indians who belong to the Catholic faith are forced to go to a Protestant school. They claim their children should not have to do this. There is great trouble with the church over this matter. I will not make any personal remarks about it but will simply say I think it is high time that the government of Canada recognize its responsibility-I know the department is doing a lot-in providing a
5910	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration proper education for these people. The government should take over the whole management of education for Indian children and not leave it for somebody else.
As there are many more who wish to speak I shall end my remarks by reminding the minister that the Canadian Citizenship Act needs a lot of review and many amendments. People concerned in cases like those I have mentioned have every right to expect a further hard, close look to be taken at their cases. They should receive the benefit of any doubt that may exist in anybody's mind, especially in the minds of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, for whom I have the greatest regard for very many reasons.
