Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I should like to refer also to the original citizens of this country. Although the problems of Indians on reservations are similar throughout the whole of Canada, I should like to deal particularly with those in my area. One reserve, for example, contains some of the best farming land in the world and yet if the government is really looking for a depressed area they need look no farther. In recent years the population has been increasing rapidly. There is not enough farm land to go round and this situation will, of course, get worse.
Like people of any other racial origin, these people are not all interested in farming, nor are they all suited to it. Yet there is no other industry or technical training available. Many of the young men have great mechanical ability. They keep old wrecks of cars running week after week when I doubt that any of us could even start one of them. If training in mechanics was available to them they might make a good living in this or related fields.
Many of these families are attempting to make a living on a quarter section with little or no equipment and little chance of ever obtaining any. Certainly the land is not at fault, because many farmers in the same area have done very well on the same amount of land. I feel that the staff of the agency is very efficient. The farm supervisor is doing a fine job but the paper work alone in his office keeps him busy. It is a full time job. I have always felt that one farm would almost keep a supervisor busy, so how can he possibly give personal attention to so many units? These units need more personal attention than any other farming units.
At present much of the land has been leased to neighbouring farmers with large equipment. The leases are ordinarily for six years. If the land has not been broken, of course, the man who leases it retains the first two crops in


the first two years. After that he turns the Indian's share into the band fund, ostensibly so that the Indian may, at the end of this six-year period, draw on this money to buy machinery to farm the land he owns. What he does, of course, in the six years he is waiting is sometimes a mystery to me. There is seasonal work available, naturally, on the surrounding farms, but this is rather on a piecemeal basis.
The new housing project seems to have been quite successful on this particular reserve. I remember that many years ago the housing situation was rather bad. The big problem, of course, is the low income of the people who must pay for these houses. Provisions for education are fairly adequate. However, I should like to point out one thing in this connection. The large Indian school on this reserve, an otherwise modern school with an enrolment of some 630 pupils, has no provision for an auditorium or a gymnasium, playroom or what have you. The weather in central Alberta, as you all know, is quite extreme at times. What do you do with that many pupils at recess or lunch hour when they cannot be turned outside? I might point out that eight miles away, in the city of Wetaskiwin, there are many schools and each one has an auditorium and a gymnasium. However, these Indian children are expected to grow up to be good citizens and to compete in our society.
I should like to mention hospitalization. For many years, the Indians have had their own hospital in the town of Hobbema, which is a village on this reserve. They were very pleased with this set-up. The more serious cases were sent to the city of Wetaskiwin or the city of Edmonton for treatment. When a new hospital was built in Wetaskiwin, it was decided that the third floor would be maintained for the benefit of the Indians, whether they liked it or not and the Hobbema hospital would be closed. I can assure you they did not like it, because they told me so. The opinion of these people had not even been asked. To be fair, of course, I should say the Hobbema hospital is still being held open as a clinic. It took a little persuasion to make this possible.
The chief objection from the standpoint of the Indians in so far as the new scheme is concerned is the additional travelling distance. Do not forget that to these people travel presents a real problem. The Indians also worry about going to a city hospital when they cannot be dressed as well as the other patients. Believe me, this is something about which they are genuinely worried.
May I suggest to the minister that when he visits some of our Indian reserves he cover the entire reserve area rather than

being content to be shown some of the more prosperous areas. He should demand to see the other areas, and perhaps then he will get a better picture of conditions as they really are.

Mr. Chairman, I have read the minister's speeches and I have listened to his speeches in the house. As a result of that, I have informed a good many of my constituents in reply to correspondence relating to citizenship and immigration that the minister is apparently a human being and we can expect some results in the near future. I do hope that my optimism in that respect will be justified.
I want to say a few words in support of the excellent representations made by previous speakers from this group in respect of the need for an overhaul of the Immigration Act. I think that is very necessary if we are going to give justice to the many Canadian citizens who try, throughout the years, to bring relatives to this country. I can think of a good number of cases, and I am going to mention three cases to illustrate the necessity for amending the act, which illustrate the necessity of overcoming some of the rigidity in the act which causes some injustice to Canadian citizens.
There is an old Chinese gentleman who lives in my district who has had a market garden for some 40 years. He is respected by everybody, and he is getting on in years. He wanted to bring his son from Hong Kong to take his place and to do some carpentry work, things of that sort. I know the case is now being reconsidered. He has received a great deal of sympathy from the people in the area, and dozens and dozens of people have signed a petition urging the government to give favourable consideration to this case. They really believe this is a case which justifies favourable consideration.
Then, there is the case of Miss Irene Rebrin, which is still sort of hanging in the air. If I remember correctly the minister made a statement in respect of several cases -and this was one of them-about the middle of December, stating that a decision would soon be made. I hope this young woman will soon be relieved of her fears, and of the uncertainty that she has from day to day by a favourable decision on the part of the department. She is doing excellent work at the University of British Columbia as a lecturer in languages.
There is another case-I am only going to mention these two cases-which indicates the necessity for amending the act in various ways. There is a Miss Sarah Eichorn who came to the Kootenays some three or four years ago from the United States. She was doing excellent work in the Kootenay school 28902-5-376J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of art, a school operated by the Society of Friends. She had had some illness and some difficulties in the United States, but she had overcome these prior to coming to Canada and establishing herself in the Kootenays. Her work was recognized by everybody interested in that type of work. Then, she went back to the United States for a period, and when she wished to return she was told she could not return because she could not qualify under certain sections of the Immigration Act. This caused great concern to the many people who had come to know this woman during her relatively short stay in the Kootenays. I understand she is not allowed to return as a visitor to obtain her personal possessions and that sort of thing. I hope every consideration will be given to a case like this. These are three cases that illustrate the necessity for an overhaul of the act, and a removal of some of these rigidities.
I am rising to speak on one other matter particularly, because during recent years I have had some unfortunate situations brought to my attention in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, largely as a result of the fact that there are two agencies of government trying to place persons in employment. The first is the national employment service, and the second is the immigration branch agency in the district. Now, the national employment service knows the needs of employers in each district. Applications for employees are turned in to the national employment service, and the officers know where different types of men can be placed. However, they are somewhat restricted as to travel.
This is what happens: The immigration officer in the district is notified-this is what has happened in the past in any event-that there will be 30 or 40 immigrants arriving at a certain time. He is asked to find employment for them. He has the right to travel all over his district. He goes to some employers and says, can you take one of these people? Often the employer has already sent in an application to the national employment service for an employee. However, the immigration officer is on his doorstep and says, can you place one of these people? The employer says, all right, send him along. He is just about to send in an application to the national employment service for an employee, and he does not do so because the immigration officer is visiting. I want to give these officers credit. They are pretty active people who know the districts well, and they go all over them.
But this is the result. Because these two agencies seek to fill applications for employment certain difficulties occur. I can give one illustration of something which has occurred
5912	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration on a number of occasions. In one of the small communities in my constituency a veteran born in the community, married and with four children, had been unemployed for seven or eight months. He was an electrician. He had turned in his application to the national employment service and visited its office nearly every day in an effort to get employment. Then an immigrant came in on the train, and the second day he was there the immigration officer found him employment in an identical position which this man had been seeking. He just happened to go to an employer who was short of a man that day.
One cannot blame the immigrant, but circumstances such as this can create a lot of unnecessary ill will and conditions that are most unfair to Canadian citizens, and to the immigrants directly concerned. In my opinion placement for employment should be undertaken by one government agency only, and that is the national employment service. Their officers know each district, the needs of employers, and where there is an opportunity to place a person. Incidents like the one I have mentioned have caused quite serious embarrassment to the officers in the service, and a lot of irritation at times.
What we require first of all is planned immigration. We should bring immigrants to this country only as they can be absorbed into employment, except in those relatively few cases where relatives undertake to be responsible for their maintenance for a period of time. We need a planned immigration policy, but we cannot have a planned immigration policy unless it is based on a planned economy, where we know the needs for employees, the needs of certain industries, so that we can bring the immigrants into Canada as they are required.
I mention this because it has occurred a number of times in my constituency and has been the cause of considerable unnecessary ill will. I urge the minister to have a look at this situation, where we have two agencies of government seeking to place persons in employment and working at cross purposes in many cases. I urge that this matter be investigated to see if something can be done to have placement in employment put directly in the hands, and only in the hands of the national employment service.

When the minister replies I hope he will deal with some citizens in my area who have been refused citizenship. On a number of occasions I have written to him respecting one particular case, which I also raised on the floor of the house. I presume the trouble has to do with security risks.
Subsequent to certain actions that were taken here by some hon. members of the

house, the Prime Minister announced that there would be a board of appeal of some kind, quasi judicial, or otherwise. Since then I have asked the Minister of Justice how a member should go about bringing a case to this board of appeal, and he told me all I needed to do was write to him and he would initiate the action that would give this particular person an opportunity to present himself and have the matter cleared up.
I have done that. I have written to the minister of immigration on a number of occasions, but so far I have had no response from him, the Minister of Justice, or the Prime Minister that they are in fact going to hear this case. When he replies I would like him to tell me what I should do now.

I am going to confine my remarks entirely to Indian affairs and because many of the things I might have said have already been said by the hon. member for Skeena, my speech will be that much briefer. The minister in his opening statement set forth a number of objectives with which most members of the committee can agree. Generally speaking I feel we should move in the direction he outlined. However, listening to him, my reaction was that life is going on with the Indian people of our country, and the state of affairs from which the minister suggested we should be moving away has existed for a long time. For example, it existed during the hearings of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Indian affairs in 1960 and 1961.
When the report of that committee was made public the Indian people in my area thought it had practically become law. I was not a member of this house at that time, but here we are almost at the end of 1963, and once more a minister is outlining some of the objectives which were set forth in the recommendations of that committee. Therefore while I am pleased, as many hon. members have been, with the ideas expressed by the minister, nevertheless I regret, even though he has not been in office many months, that he has not taken steps to institute what I would term a crash program.
As I say, the life of the Indian people goes on and their suffering continues, with its wastage of human talents. I am pleased to note that in supplementary estimates A, there are some supplementary votes devoted to matters of immediate concern to Indian affairs, but I would suggest that these moneys are a long way from being adequate. In correspondence I have tried to point out some of the inadequacies. At this stage of the discussion and at this late hour I will not outline them here, but I would like to give one illustration.

Under the west coast agency there is quite a number of Indian villages where housing conditions are appalling-and that is a mild word to describe the conditions. Some of these votes provide assistance for the development of better housing, but the funds being made available will hardly provide for the building of one house in each of these villages. Each of the villages needs more new houses than the entire agency can provide with its current level of funds. Therefore people will have to go on living in houses through which the wind blows and into which the rain seeps; and the rain sometimes does come down rather heavily on the west coast of Vancouver island.
That is just one little instance of what I describe as the inadequacies of what the people in the field can do with the funds, the sinews of war, with which we in this parliament are providing them. I could not agree more than I do with some of the suggestions and statements that have come from hon. members in this discussion, and we would like to see the end of the whole Indian affairs branch. The sooner, the better. When the hon. member for Northwest Territories suggested a 20 year plan, I think he was outlining a very realistic and worth-while program which many of us could support. But that, I submit, does not mean we should in any way seek to avoid dealing with the immediate situation.
This is why I would urge the minister to bring in, if he can, some further supplementary estimates for this work. I say that because I believe that in so many ways now the Indian people are just on the verge of a real breakthrough into a new era, and something in the way of a crash program at this time, with the understanding that the field people in his department know what they can do with it, could go a long way toward tipping the scales in the right direction to make the Indians willing and eager to become economically self-sufficient.
The hon. member for Skeena made reference to the welfare arrangement that came into effect in British Columbia on January 1 this year. I am not going to attempt to add to what he said, except to point out that because of the remaining disparities which exist in this matter, one of the effects has been that many of the Indian people are trying to move off the reserves and are creating an aggravated situation in the urban areas. I know of examples of Indian people who are ill-prepared for urban living and who are in effect becoming social delinquents because this particular half measure has been instituted between the federal and provincial authorities.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
There is one other matter to which I should like to draw particular attention. The minister suggested in his opening remarks that we should be moving in the direction of providing for Indian people various public services on the basis that applies to the rest of the Canadian people, with particular reference to having the provinces assume a wider measure of responsibility in the fields of education, health and welfare, and so on. I would suggest that if we are to have federal-provincial conferences in this field, if we are to move in this direction with the provinces, perhaps one of the things we need is an interdepartmental conference among the various departments of the federal government, because I think the federal government should be providing a lead in this connection before it starts expecting the provinces to move along with them.
By way of illustration of what I mean I should like to refer to a letter which I wrote to the Minister of Public Works earlier this year. In this letter I asked him to have an investigation made into the provision of certain improvements to the harbour installations at Opitsat village on the west coast of Vancouver island. I will not go into the details of the particular proposal that I made, because they are not relevant to the point I want to make. I received a reply from the minister, dated October 22, which reads as follows:
Opitsat, B.C.
Dear Mr. Barnett,
Thank you for your letter of October 15, 1963, in which you make some suggestions for improving the float landing facilities at Opitsat, B.C.
This department does not maintain a public landing at this place. It is my understanding that Opitsat is an Indian settlement and that the landing there was provided by the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Your letter has, therefore, been referred to that department for consideration and reply.
I might add, Mr. Chairman, that I have received since then a letter from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration saying he will have this matter looked into. But the point I am making is that if we are going to talk about provincial responsibility for Indian education, there should be federal responsibility through the Department of Public Works for federal public works in Indian settlements, the same as there is for every other settlement in this country. This is not a new matter that I am raising. In fact, I think the Secretary of State will recall that a number of years ago when he was minister of citizenship and immigration I asked him what the policy of the government was in this connection, because at that time-and
5914	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration this is apparently still the case-some installations for Indian villages were built by the public works department and others, as this correspondence reveals, were, and are, provided through funds of the Indian affairs branch. Apparently there is still no federal government policy in this connection. I would suggest this is one of the areas in which we should move to eliminate the kind of discrimination and disparity in the provision of public services to Indian people.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of things to say, but there are other members of this group who would like to speak, and obviously we cannot finish by six o'clock. I would therefore be quite happy if we could call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let us go on for a few
minutes, if the hon. member has a short speech to make. We are willing to listen to him very patiently.
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I assume the minister is going to reply at some time or other. Certainly a number of matters have been raised upon which the committee will want to hear the minister's views and the replies the minister is likely to make to the various suggestions that have been put forward. I doubt if we could have that reply, plus any other statements, in the short time that is left.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, let us sit for one hour. That is long enough.
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I think there was general agreement earlier in the day that at six o'clock it would be six o'clock, unless a moment or two would suffice to finish the business. I myself would be quite agreeable to pass the estimates, but the minister has not had a chance to reply. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is wont at all times to perhaps spend the afternoon napping in his office and then come down here and suggest that we should sit on.
If you would spend some time in the house, it would be a lot better.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege-
Six o'clock.
Let us call it six o'clock.

Well, Mr. Chairman, they are saying it is six o'clock now. The hon. member for Perth said that if I spent some time in the house, things would be better. I would like to point out that the hon. member for


Perth is a member of the privileges and
elections committee, and the only time he attended that committee was to come in and defeat a legitimate request by the people on that committee which would have done something sensible for this country.
Mr. Chairman, on the question of privilege, I would like to state that I was present at the meetings of that committee more than the one time to which the hon. member has referred.

If it is the wish of the committee to continue this debate, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that tomorrow we sit for the same hours as we sat today. I think any hon. member would be quite agreeable to continuing this debate tomorow.
Shame.

I would suggest that those who are saying "shame" should have a little understanding of the fact that the Hansard reporters, the translators and others have had an exceptionally difficult week, one which would not be allowed anywhere else. If we had a regular day's sitting tomorrow, hon. members might be agreeable to participate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I assume, Mr. Chairman, that if I attempted the unusual role of peacemaker I would not get very far; but if total abstinence would appeal to a few hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house, and if the minister were permitted about five minutes to make a brief reply, perhaps we could pass these estimates and we could then start something fresh at the next sitting.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But I am not pressing that point at all. If there is any objection from any quarter the hon. member for Skeena is quite right. We got agreement to sit till six o'clock and I would not suggest anything more.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that there is so much more legislation to be dealt with before prorogation surely you can get unanimous consent to sit another half hour, even if that is necessary. I say this because I know the N.D.P. would not dare obstruct, as I have before me a letter written by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to his constituents blaming the Conservative party for obstruction in this house. We have never been guilty of that and are prepared to sit tonight for the next half hour.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: If that letter is to be referred to I trust that the hon. member will read the entire letter; otherwise it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not after six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that the committee continue?
Agreed.
Six o'clock.

Obstruction.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe there would be a disposition on the part of the house to make an order now that on Monday next we sit until 10.30 instead of ten o'clock; that on Tuesday next we sit until 10.30 rather than ten o'clock; that if we complete the legislation that the government puts forward on those two days and there is any time left before 10.30 on either day the house would agree to go into committee of supply without question put; and that on Wednesday we would sit till seven o'clock. If my understanding of the will of the house is correct, I hope that that would be made an order of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We agree.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: This is in accordance with our understanding and we agree.
We are in agreement with that plan.
We also agree, Mr. Speaker. [Text]

Mr. Speaker, I think it should be understood that when we agree to these hours they should be kept. This constant business of trying to extend the hours another half hour or an hour is unfair to members who have stayed faithfully throughout the entire period. I think that if we agree to these hours we should adhere to them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to think that there is nothing but free consent in these matters and that that question would not arise.
The Aciing Speaker (Mr. Batten): Is it
agreed that the hours of sitting next week be extended in accordance with the statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill)?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It is so
ordered.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Will the Secretary of State tell us what we are to fit into those hours?
Business of the House

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will be glad to tell the house what I should like to have fitted into those hours. I should like the house to find it possible on Monday to deal with the bill respecting the representation commissioner, I hope in all its stages; with the bill respecting the Customs Tariff; with the bill respecting salaries; with the bill respecting the national centennial; with the bill respecting C.N.R. financing; and with both the resolution and the bill respecting the world's fair.
In addition to that there are four bills which have already come from the Senate, three of them relating to the Department of Transport and one abolishing the Newfoundland Savings Bank, which has not existed for several years anyway, all of which we should like at some time during the week to get passed. They might be held over till after all the estimates have been passed to be dealt with during the interval while the other place is considering the appropriation bill. Those ten legislative items-the first six of which the government feels are essential, and the four Senate bills-we feel desirable to dispose of, and I do not think they are too controversial.
There are two other items on the order paper which might be taken if time could be found for them. One is the aeronautics bill, which is pretty well through incidentally, and the other the bill relating to provincial taxes; but the government would not hold up prorogation if neither of these measures is even touched during the week, much less completed.
On Wednesday, as I indicated last night, it is our thought that we should start with the eagerly anticipated estimates of the Postmaster General. About an hour later, when they have been completed we would take the Speaker's estimates, for which there seems to be some desire. We would also try on Wednesday to complete the Department of National Revenue. Some other departments would be available as well for the last hour or two after those have been completed on Wednesday.
As for the estimates for the other two days of the week I think it would be desirable to have some consultation when we have made more progress.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, could we perhaps get the sense of the house now with respect to the suggestion that we dispense with the debate on the notice of motion in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau) regarding the Indian claims commission in order that the bill may be introduced?

Business of the House

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In view of the debate which has taken place on the minister's estimates, if it was the desire to sit for another few minutes so that Mr. Speaker could leave the chair to go into committee to consider that motion, and then have the bill introduced, I think it would expedite matters a great deal and would be very much appreciated.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Bring it forward in the regular way on one of the other days.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Let us do it now.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why wait for spring?
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: When the leader of the house was announcing the business for next week I did not hear him mention the estimates of the Department of Industry. I believe there was a suggestion that they might be up for consideration on Tuesday. I see the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount shakes his head, but I believe the Secretary of State did say something to that effect. He knows the importance of this. The people of Nova Scotia are anxiously awaiting a statement by the Minister of Industry on the heavy water situation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I share the concern which the hon. member feels about this matter and every endeavour will be made to bring the estimates of the Department of Industry back again before the committee as soon as it

is possible for the minister to say something constructive about that matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISPOSITION OF INDIAN CLAIMS

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Favreau (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISPOSITION OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the disposition of Indian claims and in relation thereto,-
1.	To provide for the establishment of an Indian claims commission:
2.	To provide for the duties of the commission, its decisions and awards;
3.	To provide for appeals from the decisions of the commission to the Indian claims appeal court; and
4.	To enact such financial provisions as may be necessary to accomplish the purposes of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Favreau thereupon moved for leave to present Bill No. C-130, to provide for the disposition of Indian claims.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISPOSITION OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: Now we have made this concession, may we revert to committee of supply and go on with the estimates of the department?
It being fourteen minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
Monday, December 16, 1963
